The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

In chapter 9 we described vibration with one degree of freedom by a viscous damper, and in chapter 10 we carried this over to several degrees of freedom and chose the damping so that the modes still decoupled. We used all of it with one silent assumption: the damper exists and has a known constant. This chapter tests that assumption. It also builds on chapter 3, which promised that a material does not return all its work, and on the chapters on finite elements (7, 12).

The word damping (dušenje) means everything that takes energy from a vibration, so that the amplitude fades with time. The word model means a simplified description that we can put into a calculation: a rule for how the force we feel as damping depends on displacement and velocity. In a viscous damper the force is proportional to the velocity. In friction in a clamp the force always has the same magnitude and changes direction when the motion reverses. In the inside of steel the force on unloading is smaller than on loading at the same elongation, so the graph of force against elongation closes a loop in one cycle. Damping models are therefore different rules for the same experience, that a vibration dies out. The real causes differ and often act together, but into a calculation we put one rule that stands in for them.

Why does it matter? A cantilever carrying a mass of 50 kg, struck once, loses some energy in every period, yet no damper hangs under it. A machine on rubber mounts passes a smaller force into the ground when the mounts are soft, and when the rotor turns far above resonance, damping in the mounts can make this worse. A two-storey frame with one damper between the ground and the first floor has a vibration that classical damping cannot describe. In each of these cases the choice of model changes the number the designer gets.

The chapter promises to test the damping model every time, not merely assume it. First we find a measure that lets us compare all the causes, namely the energy a vibration loses in one period. Then we show when another cause may be replaced by a viscous damper and when not, and how damping that arises in the material behaves under vibration at one frequency. Next we describe a material that responds slowly to a load, first with models made of springs and dampers, then with the history of the load. Finally we put this into finite elements, write the vibration in a form that also gives damping that the classical model cannot describe, and look at the damping of a beam and of a string.

20.1 Where the energy of a vibration goes and how we measure it

Cantilever A does come to rest after a blow, and in chapter 9 we described this with a viscous damper, chosen so that \(\zeta = 0{,}01\). No real damper hangs on it. So what does take the energy, and how do we compare causes as different as friction in the clamp, the air around the mass and the inside of the steel? This section looks for one common measure, with which we shall judge every model in the following sections.

Let us draw cantilever A (example 9.9). The bar is clamped into the wall, which is tied to the ground. At its end is the mass \(m\), which after a blow moves up and down with velocity \(\dot q\). Three things can take energy. The first is the joint at the wall: two plates and two bolts hold the bar, and at every swing it slips a little against the plates. The force of dry friction has constant size and points against the slip (section 9.14 of chapter 9, theorem 9.150), so during slip it takes energy. We draw the force \(f_{\mathrm{t}}\) as a double arrow in the gap between plate and bar, because the slip changes direction as the bar swings. The second is the air: the mass pushes the air in front of it, and by the law of action and reaction (Newton's third law) the air pushes the mass back with an equal force. When the mass moves up, the air acts on its top face downwards, so the force \(f_{\mathrm{z}}\) is drawn downwards and ends on that face. The third is the material of the bar. The bar bends as it swings, every piece of steel is stretched and compressed, and this loss is there without joints and without air. TIMO (PDF p. 297) says that there are systems in which the damping of vibration depends mainly on the internal friction (notranje trenje) of the material.

Which of the three prevails in A, these words do not tell. We only know that all three have the same consequence: in every period the vibration loses some energy. That consequence can be measured whatever the cause, and it will be our common measure. First, though, let us see what happens in the material, where no layer slides.

20.1.1 Loss in the material: heat between grains

What loses energy in a piece of steel that we stretch and release? TIMO (PDF pp. 295, 296) describes an experiment with a crystal that is stretched with a pulling force while its temperature is observed.

On the axes we measure the elongation \(q\) horizontally and the pulling force \(P\) vertically. When we pull very slowly, the crystal keeps the temperature of its surroundings all the time, and the force grows along the dashed line \(0\) to \(2\), whose slope is proportional to the modulus of elasticity at constant temperature (the isothermal modulus \(E_{\mathrm{iz}}\), definition 3.1). When we pull quickly, no heat escapes and the crystal cools. The quick pull is the segment \(0\) to \(1\), with a larger slope, the adiabatic modulus \(E_{\mathrm{ad}} > E_{\mathrm{iz}}\) (adiabatic means without exchange of heat). Why the larger slope? The cooled bar wants to contract, as a steel rail contracts in winter, so under the same force it is shorter than the warm one: at the corner \(1\) the elongation is smaller than at \(2\) at the same height, and the difference is the segment \(1\) to \(2\). So only a larger force brings it to the same elongation. At \(1\) we stop and hold the force constant. The cooled bar slowly warms to the temperature of its surroundings and therefore stretches a little more, which is the horizontal line \(1\) to \(2\). Now we release the load suddenly. The bar contracts along the line \(2\) to \(3\), parallel to \(0\) to \(1\), because this contraction again has no exchange of heat. It warms up in doing so, so after the release it cools to the temperature of its surroundings and contracts a further segment \(3\) to \(0\). The cycle returns to its start and is a parallelogram. At the corner \(3\) the force is zero but the elongation still positive, so the parallelogram leans to the right.

Why is the area of the parallelogram a loss of energy? The work we do on the bar at elongation \(q\) and force \(P\) is the time integral of \(P\,\dot q\), and this is the area under the graph of \(P\) against \(q\) (fundamental theorem of calculus, theorem 3.55). On loading the graph lies above the graph on unloading, so the difference of the two areas is the area of the parallelogram. We prove this in detail in the next section (lemma 20.2). The bar acts with force \(-P\) on whatever pulls it (Newton's third law), in vibration on the mass. So in these axes the loop of the force on the mass is turned over compared with figure 20.5, but the area is the same. This energy does not go into the bar as elastic energy, since after the cycle the bar is back in the same state. It ends as heat that the bar gives to its surroundings. TIMO (PDF p. 296) writes that the difference between the adiabatic and the isothermal modulus is usually small, for steel about a third of one per cent (footnote 1 on the same page), so the loss of energy per cycle is very small too, but in vibration many cycles follow one another, and such losses are what is called internal friction and damp the motion. In reality heat is exchanged all the time, and instead of the parallelogram we get a rounded loop.

How small is "very small" for steel? Let us count on figure 20.4. The parallelogram has the base \(1\) to \(2\) and the height \(P\). The stiffness of the bar is proportional to the modulus, so for \(E_{\mathrm{ad}} = (1 + 1/300)\,E_{\mathrm{iz}}\) the elongation at \(1\) is \(q_2/(1 + 1/300)\), where \(q_2\) is the elongation at \(2\), and the base is \(q_2/301\). The area of the parallelogram is therefore \(P\,q_2/301\), and the elastic energy under the dashed line up to \(2\) is \(\tfrac12 P\,q_2\). In this cycle \(2/301 = 0{,}66\ \%\) of the stored energy is lost (the calculation is ours, from the number in the footnote). The figure therefore exaggerates the difference of the slopes strongly: to scale, the parallelogram would be narrower than the line it is drawn with.

Steel is not a single crystal but many grains with differently oriented crystal lattices. TIMO (PDF pp. 296, 297) says that the cooling during stretching depends on the orientation of the crystal, so temperatures differ from grain to grain. The figure shows two grains with temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\). The grain with the lower temperature \(T_2\) is shaded more strongly, the grain \(T_1\) is cooled less. Heat flows from the warmer to the colder grain across their common boundary, the arrow, and the temperatures even out. This is an additional flow of heat, which a single crystal would not have, and it increases the loss of energy.

How can the loss be increased? By TIMO (PDF p. 297) the heat generated in a grain is proportional to its volume and the exchange of heat to its surface, so the evening out is easier and the loss larger when the grains are made smaller. Let us count on a cube of side \(2d\) and on the same cube cut into eight cubes of side \(d\), drawn in the plane as a square and four squares. The volume is \(8d^3\) in both cases. The surface of the whole cube is \(6\,(2d)^2 = 24\,d^2\), the surface of the eight cubes \(8 \cdot 6d^2 = 48\,d^2\). The surface across which heat flows is thus twice as large when the grains are twice as small. In the plane of the figure the perimeter \(8d\) grows to \(16d\) in the same way. That is why, in systems whose damping depends mainly on the internal friction of the material, we increase the damping with a material of small grains (TIMO, PDF p. 297).

From history

Losses of energy in metals were measured before their cause was known. TIMO (PDF p. 297, footnote 1) reports that the damping capacity (zmožnost dušenja) of various materials was measured by Rowett (1913), and later by Otto Föppl and his collaborators at the Wöhler Institute in Brunswick (1926 to 1929). A measurement tells how much energy a material loses, not where. The importance of the thermoelastic cause of internal friction was shown by the investigations of C. Zener and his associates (1937 to 1941), that is, the flow of heat of figure 20.4. Zener collected the results in the book "Elasticity and Anelasticity of Metals" (1948).

Let us return to the grains and the loop in the material of figure 20.4. All three causes of figure 20.3 have the same consequence: the force that the member exerts on the mass is not a function of the displacement alone, but differs on loading and on unloading. We now write this down exactly.

20.1.2 Work in a period is the area of the loop

What should we measure? The loss of energy in one period of the motion, because this is a number that can be read off a graph of force against displacement whatever the cause. Take one degree of freedom with mass \(m\), coordinate \(q\) and a member that acts on the mass with force \(f\) in the direction of \(q\) (a spring, a damper, a joint or the material, or all at once). Chapter 9 did this for the damper.

Definition 20.1 Energy lost per period (izguba energije v periodi)

Let \(q(t)\) be a continuously differentiable motion with period \(T > 0\), that is \(q(t + T) = q(t)\), and \(f(t)\) a piecewise continuous force (definition 6.8), with which the member acts on the mass in the direction of \(q\), and which also has period \(T\). The energy lost per period (izguba energije v periodi) is the number

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^T f(t)\,\dot q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{20.1}\]

that is, minus the work of the force \(f\) in one period (definition 8.59, the power is \(f\,\dot q\)). The unit is the joule. In the figure of loops it is the shaded area in (b).

Source: Loss per period as the work of the damping force: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 126), equations (4.70) and (4.72). The definition with a sign that makes the loss of a damper positive is ours.

Why this name? When the mass is in the same state after a period, it has the same velocity, so the total work of all forces on it in the period is zero. From \(m\,\ddot q = f + Q\), where \(Q\) is the external force, we get after multiplying by \(\dot q\) and integrating over the period \(\big[\tfrac12 m\,\dot q^2\big]_0^T = 0 = \int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t + \int_0^T Q\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\) (fundamental theorem, theorem 3.55). The external force thus supplies exactly \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period, as the loop of the driving force shows. This is the energy that a force must keep supplying for the motion to stay periodic, as at resonance in chapter 9 (theorem 9.73).

Now let us draw \(f\) against \(q\) over one period. For the damper this is the ellipse of figure 9.83. We ask the same question of every member we know.

We draw the axes: the displacement \(q\) horizontally and the force \(f\) vertically, in each of the four panels. First the spring. Its force is \(-kq\) and it is a single line, since on rising and on falling at the same \(q\) it acts the same. The loop has no area, so a spring loses no energy at any amplitude. In (b) we add a viscous damper: the total force \(-kq - c\,\dot q\) runs along an ellipse, tilted by the spring (the dashed line \(-kq\) is its axis), and the shaded area is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\). The ellipse is run through counter-clockwise. In (c) is dry friction: on rising the force is \(-F_{\mathrm{t}}\), on falling \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so the loop is a rectangle with sides \(2X\) and \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\). In (d) is the driving force \(Q_0\cos\Omega t\) at resonance against the displacement \(X\sin\Omega t\). This too is an ellipse, but it is run through clockwise, while the damping force runs the other way. Why does the direction matter? Because the area with its sign is the work, as the lemma that follows proves.

We prove the statement for every motion in which the displacement rises once and falls once in a period. Harmonic motion is such, since the point goes round one loop. For others, for instance with two peaks in a period, the curve of force against displacement can make several loops, definition 20.1 still holds, only reading off a single area is lost.

Let us draw the idea of the proof before we write it. Take the axes \(q\) and \(f\) as before and a loop that is neither an ellipse nor a rectangle, so that we use nothing special. In (a) the displacement goes from \(-X\) to \(X\) and the point \((q, f)\) runs to the right along the lower branch \(F_\uparrow\). The work of the force on this way is the area under the branch, because the displacement grows and the force is positive (we drew the branches above the axis so that the areas can be seen, the lemma does not require it). The upper branch is only dashed here, because we do not walk along it yet. In (b) the displacement returns from \(X\) to \(-X\) along the upper branch \(F_\downarrow\), and the lower one is dashed. The force points the same way as before but the displacement the opposite way, so the work is negative: minus the area under the upper branch. In (c) we add the two works. The part under the lower branch enters once with a plus and once with a minus and cancels. What remains is minus the area between the branches: the work of the force in a period is minus the area of the loop, and the loss \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the area of the loop. The point went round the loop counter-clockwise. A narrow upright strip at one \(q\) has the height \(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow\), and the area of the loop is made of such strips. The lemma says this precisely, and the proof justifies every step by the fundamental theorem.

Lemma 20.2 Work in a period and the area of the loop (delo v periodi in ploščina zanke)

Let \(q\) be a continuously differentiable function with period \(T\) that strictly increases on \([0, t_1]\) from \(-X\) to \(X\) and strictly decreases on \([t_1, T]\) from \(X\) to \(-X\), with \(X > 0\). Let \(f\) be piecewise continuous and let there be continuous functions \(F_\uparrow\), \(F_\downarrow\) on \([-X, X]\) with \(f(t) = F_\uparrow(q(t))\) for \(0 \le t < t_1\) and \(f(t) = F_\downarrow(q(t))\) for \(t_1 < t < T\). Then:

  1. \(\displaystyle\int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\big(F_\uparrow(q) - F_\downarrow(q)\big)\,\mathrm{d}q\). This is the difference of the area under the lower branch and the area under the upper branch.
  2. If \(F_\downarrow \ge F_\uparrow\) on \([-X, X]\), then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the area between the graphs of \(F_\downarrow\) and \(F_\uparrow\), that is the area of the loop that the point \((q(t), f(t))\) goes round counter-clockwise. If \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\), then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is minus the area of the loop that the point goes round clockwise, and the member supplies energy.
  3. If we add the same continuous function \(G(q)\) to both branches, the integral in item 1 does not change. In particular, a force \(f = G(q)\) that depends on the displacement alone (a spring) has \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0\).
Proof

We must show three items. The first we get by recognizing on each branch the integral as a difference of values of an antiderivative, the second from the meaning of the difference of graphs, the third from item 1.

  1. Let \(\Phi_\uparrow(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{y} F_\uparrow(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), which is the area under the lower branch from \(-X\) to \(y\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55, item 2) \(\Phi_\uparrow\) is differentiable with derivative \(F_\uparrow\), because \(F_\uparrow\) is continuous.
  2. On the open interval \((0, t_1)\), that is on the way up, the values \(q(t)\) lie in the open interval \((-X, X)\), where \(\Phi_\uparrow\) has the continuous derivative \(F_\uparrow\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.30, item 3) the function \(t \mapsto \Phi_\uparrow(q(t))\) is therefore differentiable on \((0, t_1)\) with derivative \(F_\uparrow(q(t))\,\dot q(t)\). The function is continuous on \([0, t_1]\), being a composition of continuous functions, and its derivative extends continuously to \([0, t_1]\), being a product of continuous functions.
  3. By the fundamental theorem (item 1) \(\int_0^{t_1} F_\uparrow(q)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \Phi_\uparrow(q(t_1)) - \Phi_\uparrow(q(0)) = \Phi_\uparrow(X) - \Phi_\uparrow(-X) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X} F_\uparrow(q)\,\mathrm{d}q\), because \(\Phi_\uparrow(-X) = 0\). This is the whole area in (a).
  4. On the falling branch, with \(\Phi_\downarrow(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{y} F_\downarrow\), we get in the same way \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{T} F_\downarrow(q)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \Phi_\downarrow(q(T)) - \Phi_\downarrow(q(t_1)) = \Phi_\downarrow(-X) - \Phi_\downarrow(X) = -\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X} F_\downarrow\,\mathrm{d}q\). The minus comes from going from \(X\) back to \(-X\): this is the area in (b) with a minus.
  5. The points \(t_1\) and \(T\) do not change the integral (definition 6.9), so the sum of steps 3 and 4 is item 1, picture (c).
  6. For item 2, \(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow \ge 0\) is the height of the region between the graphs at \(q\), so \(\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow)\,\mathrm{d}q\) is its area. From item 1 and definition 20.1, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\) is this area. As \(q\) increases the point \((q, f)\) runs along the lower graph \(F_\uparrow\) from left to right, and as \(q\) decreases along the upper graph \(F_\downarrow\) from right to left, that is counter-clockwise. For \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\) the graphs are swapped and the direction reversed.
  7. For item 3, after adding \(G\) both branches are raised by the same number at every \(q\), and the difference \(F_\uparrow - F_\downarrow\) is the same. In figure 20.5 (b), \(G = -kq\) is the dashed line that tilts the ellipse. For \(F_\uparrow = F_\downarrow = G\) the difference is zero.

Source: Work of the damping force as the area of a loop: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 127, figure 4.17). The proof is not from the sources.

Let us see what the proof says, and test it on what we know. For the ellipse of chapter 9 take \(q = -X\cos\Omega t\), which increases from \(-X\) to \(X\) on \([0, T/2]\). The damper force \(-c\,\dot q = -c\,\Omega X\sin\Omega t\) equals \(F_\uparrow(q) = -c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\), because \(\sin\Omega t \ge 0\) on this branch, and on the falling branch \(F_\downarrow(q) = +c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\). The difference is \(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow = 2c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\), which by the lemma has area \(2c\,\Omega\cdot\tfrac12\pi X^2 = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), since \(\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\,\mathrm{d}q\) is the area of a half disc of radius \(X\) (the area of a disc is \(\pi X^2\)). This is exactly the loss of theorem 9.73.

The first loop of figure 20.5, the spring alone, is the case that the lemma tells apart from the damper, although \(-kq\) is also a force in the direction of \(q\). For \(-kq\) we have \(F_\uparrow = F_\downarrow = -kq\), area zero and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0\) by item 3. That is why the loop of the total force \(-kq - c\,\dot q\) in (b) has the same area as the loop of the damping force alone, the ellipse, as item 3 says: the spring only tilts the ellipse and does not change its area.

The opposite case is the driving force in (d). At resonance \(q = X\sin\Omega t\) and \(Q = Q_0\cos\Omega t\), a loop run clockwise, \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\). By item 2, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is minus the area, that is \(-\pi\,Q_0 X = -1{,}0018\) J. A member that goes round its loop in this way is not a damper but a source of energy. At resonance the driving force has exactly the same ellipse as the damping force, only in the opposite direction, which is the balance \(Q_0 = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) of chapter 9. The sign of \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) separates a damper from a source.

For a motion with two peaks in a period the hypothesis of the lemma fails already at the branches: at the same \(q\) the force can differ on the two rises, so there is no single function \(F_\uparrow\) such as the lower branch. The loss is then computed directly from equation (20.1). We need the lemma only where we want to read the number off a picture.

20.1.3 Loss factor

How do we compare the loss between systems that have different stiffnesses and amplitudes? By dividing by the energy stored in the system.

Let us draw both energies in one picture, for cantilever A at resonance and this time to scale. On the axes are the displacement \(q\) and the force \(f\) on the mass. The spring line \(-kq\) goes from \(-X\) to \(X\) and at \(X\) reaches \(1000\) N. At the largest displacement \(X\) the mass has zero velocity, all the energy is in the spring and equals \(U = \tfrac12 kX^2\), the stored energy (shranjena energija). In the picture this is the triangle between the spring line and the \(q\) axis with legs \(X\) and \(kX\), as CK shows it in figure 4.17 (PDF p. 127): the work we do when we slowly stretch the spring from \(0\) to \(X\) is the area under its force. The loop of the total force of spring and damper is hardly thicker than the line at this scale, so we magnify the middle ten times. In (b) we see that the branches of the loop run \(20\) N below the spring line and \(20\) N above it, which is the largest damper force \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\).

Why does the definition that follows divide by \(2\pi U\) and not just by \(U\)? Let us compare the two areas in figure 20.7. The loop is the ellipse of the damper with semi-axes \(X\) and \(c\,\Omega X\), which the spring only tilted without changing its area (lemma 20.2, item 3), so \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi \cdot X \cdot c\,\Omega X\). The triangle has \(U = \tfrac12 \cdot X \cdot kX\). The ratio is

\[\frac{W_{\mathrm{izg}}}{U} = 2\pi\,\frac{c\,\Omega X}{kX} .\]

The number \(2\pi\) comes from the shapes, \(\pi\) from the ellipse and \(2\) from the triangle. When we remove it, what remains is the ratio of two forces that we read off the picture: the largest damper force to the largest spring force, for A \(20/1000 = 0{,}02\). Counting phase says the same: \(2\pi\) is the number of radians in one period, so \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}/2\pi\) is the loss per radian. For a viscous damper at resonance \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 1/(2\zeta)\) (corollary 9.75), a number we already know.

Definition 20.3 Loss factor (faktor izgub)

Let the motion be periodic with amplitude \(X > 0\), let the loss per period have the value \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) (definition 20.1), and let \(k > 0\) be the stiffness of the spring that holds the mass. The loss factor (faktor izgub) is the dimensionless number

\[\gamma = \frac{W_{\mathrm{izg}}}{2\pi\,U} , \qquad U = \tfrac12 k X^2 . \tag{20.2}\]

It can depend on the mechanism, on the amplitude \(X\) and on the frequency \(\Omega\) of the motion, while the mass does not appear in the definition. In the figure of stored energy, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the loop and \(U\) the triangle.

Source: CK (4.79) (PDF p. 129) introduces \(\gamma\) as the structural damping factor and compares it with the number \(2\zeta r\) of viscous damping (PDF p. 129, (4.82), (4.83)), but does not relate it to the loss of energy. Here we derive it from the energy, and the ratio \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is that of chapter 9 (corollary 9.75).

The name says what share of the stored energy is lost: the loop is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 2\pi\gamma\,U\), where \(U\) is the triangle. In chapter 1 \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the engineering shear strain, but in this chapter \(\gamma\) is always the loss factor.

Lemma 20.4 Loss factor of a viscous damper (faktor izgub viskoznega dušilnika)

Let a system with mass \(m\), stiffness \(k\) and viscous damper \(c\) (definition 9.1) move steadily as \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\), let \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and let \(\zeta\) be the damping ratio (definition 9.5). Then

\[\gamma = \frac{c\,\Omega}{k} = 2\zeta\,r . \tag{20.3}\]

At A, \(c\,\Omega/k\) is the ratio of the largest damper force to the largest spring force. At resonance (\(r = 1\)) we have \(\gamma = 2\zeta = 1/D(1)\) with the dynamic factor \(D\) (definition 9.64), so \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 1/\gamma\) (corollary 9.75).

Proof

We must show equation (20.3) and its special case.

  1. By theorem 9.73 the loss per period is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), because the mean power lost is \(\tfrac12 c\,\Omega^2X^2\) and \(T = 2\pi/\Omega\).
  2. By definition 20.3 (loop over triangle), \(\gamma = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2/(2\pi\cdot\tfrac12 kX^2) = c\,\Omega/k\).
  3. From \(c = 2\zeta m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(k = m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) (definition 9.5) we get \(c\,\Omega/k = 2\zeta\,\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 2\zeta\,r\).
  4. At \(r = 1\), \(\gamma = 2\zeta\), and \(D(1) = 1/(2\zeta)\) by corollary 9.75.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (4.77), (4.78) (PDF p. 128) for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is the same calculation.

Let us try it on A, in figure 20.7. For viscous \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) and resonance, \(X = 15{,}944\) mm, the loop has \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 1{,}0018\) J and the triangle \(U = \tfrac12\cdot 62\,720\cdot 0{,}015944^2 = 7{,}9719\) J. So \(\gamma = 1{,}0018/(2\pi\cdot 7{,}9719) = 0{,}0200 = 2\zeta\), as the lemma says. The loss per period is \(2\pi\gamma = 12{,}6\ \%\) of the stored energy: the area of the thin loop is an eighth of the area of the triangle. Since \(\gamma = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/k = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X/(kX)\), \(1/\gamma = 50\) is also the ratio of the largest spring force \(kX = 1000\) N to the largest damper force \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 20\) N. The loop is thin and shows that the damping is small (on this rests the replacement by an equivalent viscous damper, treated in the next section). In figure 20.5 we drew it exaggeratedly wide in (b), so that the area can be seen.

Example 20.5 Loss factor of viscous damping and of friction on cantilever A (faktor izgub viskoznega dušenja in trenja pri konzoli A)

Cantilever A (\(k = 62\,720\) N/m, \(m = 50\) kg, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s) vibrates at resonance with amplitude \(X\). Its loops are the ellipse of the viscous damper and the rectangle of friction.

  1. Viscous, \(\zeta = 0{,}01\): \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 1{,}0018\) J at \(X = 15{,}944\) mm. The loss factor is \(\gamma = 0{,}0200\). At \(r = 0{,}5\) we get \(\gamma = 0{,}0100\), at \(r = 2\) we get \(0{,}0400\), at any amplitude the same (by lemma 20.4 it depends on \(r\) alone). The loop is a thin ellipse.
  2. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N: on rising \(F_\uparrow = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\), on falling \(F_\downarrow = +F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so by lemma 20.2 \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\big(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow\big)\,\mathrm{d}q = 2F_{\mathrm{t}}\cdot 2X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), the rectangle with sides \(2X\) and \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\). At \(X = 15{,}944\) mm this is \(0{,}1276\) J, and \(\gamma = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X/(\pi k X^2) = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi k X) = 0{,}00255\). That is \(12{,}7\ \%\) of the loss of the viscous damping.
  3. The same friction at smaller amplitudes: \(X = 5\) mm gives \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0{,}0400\) J, \(U = 0{,}784\) J, \(\gamma = 0{,}00812\). \(X = 1\) mm gives \(0{,}00800\) J, \(0{,}03136\) J, \(\gamma = 0{,}0406\). The friction rectangle at smaller \(X\) is lower and narrower, the triangle much smaller.

The third item shows the difference, so let us draw the numbers of the example. On the axes the amplitude \(X\) in millimetres is horizontal and the loss factor vertical. The viscous damper gives the horizontal line at \(0{,}02\), because \(\gamma\) does not depend on the amplitude. Friction gives three points: \(0{,}00255\) at \(15{,}944\) mm, \(0{,}00812\) at \(5\) mm and \(0{,}0406\) at \(1\) mm. They lie on the curve \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi kX)\), proportional to \(1/X\): the smaller the vibration, the larger the share of energy lost. Why? The rectangle of friction has the constant height \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so its area grows with \(X\) (picture (c)), while the triangle \(U\) has both legs proportional to \(X\) and grows with \(X^2\) (the triangle). At the amplitude of resonance friction is almost eight times weaker than the viscous damper, at \(X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi k\cdot 2\zeta) = 2{,}03\) mm they are equal, and below this amplitude friction prevails. So for friction there is no single number \(\gamma\), only a number at a given amplitude. The two mechanisms also differ in what they depend on: for the viscous one the loss per period is proportional to \(\Omega X^2\), for friction to \(X\) and independent of the frequency. What this means for the equation of motion and when we may replace the loop by an ellipse is told by the next section (section 20.2).

For steel itself TIMO gives no loss factor on these pages (PDF pp. 296, 297). From the difference of the moduli we got only the loss of \(0{,}66\ \%\) in the cycle with the parallelogram, which by definition 20.3 would give \(\gamma = 0{,}0066/2\pi = 0{,}0011\), almost twenty times less than \(0{,}02\) for A. This is an order of magnitude for one slow cycle, not a measurement of vibration. We shall use the loss factor to judge all the models of this chapter: the viscous one (section 20.2), the hysteretic one (section 20.3) and the viscoelastic models of the material (section 20.4).

20.2 Equivalent viscous damping

At resonance, cantilever \(A\) of section 9.1 with viscous damping \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) has amplitude \(X = 15{,}944\) mm and loses \(1{,}0018\) J in every period (theorem 9.73). In example 9.151 we added dry friction of force \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N. What is the amplitude at resonance now? The equation of motion

\[m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) = Q_0\cos\Omega t\]

is not linear, so the methods of chapter 9 do not solve it: they relied on the sum of two solutions being a solution again, and on the complex form of the harmonic response (theorem 9.62). Here we look for another way. In steady vibration the system returns to the same state after every period, with the same displacement and the same velocity, so also with the same energy. What the exciting force supplied in a period, the damping therefore had to remove in the same period (theorem 9.73). So one single property of the damping sets the amplitude: how much energy it removes in a period. How the damping force is spread within the period does not change this balance. It changes only the shape of the motion, and little: for cantilever \(A\) by \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the amplitude (section 20.2.2). If we know that number we can take it as the measure and replace the damper by a viscous one that removes the same amount. The figure shows that the energy returns to the same level after a period and that the energy supplied and the energy removed are equal.

On the horizontal axis we plot time, three periods above and one below. The upper curve is the energy of the system: in part of the period it rises, because the exciting force supplies more than the damping removes, in the other part it falls. At the start of every period it lies at the same level, which is the steady state. Below are the power supplied by the exciting force and the power removed by the damping over one period. Since the energy is no higher after a period, the two areas under the curves are equal: this is the energy balance on which this section rests.

The model is system \(A\) of section 9.1: a mass \(m = 50\) kg on a spring \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, the coordinate \(q\) is the displacement of the mass. Besides the spring force and the exciting force \(Q = Q_0\cos\Omega t\), the mass is acted on by a damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\) (N), produced by any mechanism: a viscous damper (\(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\), definition 9.1), friction, or something else. The letter \(c\) in this section always means the coefficient of a dashpot as in chapter 9, and never the wave speed of chapter 13. The assumption, which we name because it cannot be justified in advance, is that the motion is (approximately) harmonic, \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with amplitude \(X > 0\), circular frequency \(\Omega > 0\) and period \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\). Why it is right here: the damping of cantilever \(A\) is light (with friction \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}0115\)) and we excite it at resonance, so it responds strongly only to the component of the force at the fundamental frequency and hardly at all to the higher components. When it does not hold: when friction is so large or the excitation so slow that the mass sticks during a vibration. What it costs: for friction we neglect a remainder of the force that is large as a force (\(43{,}5\ \%\) of the root mean square of the friction force) but adds only \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the amplitude to the displacement. Both numbers are computed in section 20.2.2. Figure 20.10 shows the setup, and in it the damping mechanism is left unspecified.

In the figure the mass \(m\) is a block that slides horizontally on the ground, held on the left to a wall by the spring \(k\). The displacement \(q\) is measured to the right from the equilibrium position. The exciting force \(Q\) pulls to the right, the damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) to the left. It comes from the mechanism under the block, which we leave open for now: it may be a viscous damper, friction or something else.

How much energy does the mechanism remove? We already have this measure: the energy lost per period (definition 20.1) is the work of the damping force over a period with the opposite sign, where \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\) is the power of the damping force (definition 8.59). We write it once more for the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\), because we shall refer to it:

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}} f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{20.4}\]

The sign is chosen so that \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} > 0\) for every real damping that slows the motion. What does this integral mean on a plot of the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) against the displacement \(q\)? By lemma 20.2 (section 20.1), \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the area of the loop that the point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) traces in a period. We draw the loop (figure 20.11).

On the horizontal axis we plot the displacement \(q\), on the vertical axis the damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\), and with the marks \(\pm X\) we mark the extreme positions between which the mass moves. The amplitude here is \(X = 13{,}914\) mm and not \(15{,}944\) mm as for the loops of section 20.1: it is the steady amplitude of the cantilever with friction, which we compute in section 20.2.1. In dry friction the force has the constant magnitude \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\) and always points against the velocity. When the mass moves to the right (\(\dot q > 0\)), \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so this is the lower side of the rectangle from \(-X\) to \(X\). At the right end the velocity reverses and the force jumps to \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\) while the mass moves to the left, this is the upper side. The point travels around the rectangle counterclockwise, like around the ellipse of the viscous damper in figure 9.83. The area of the rectangle is the width \(2X\) times the height \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\),

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 2X\cdot 2F_{\mathrm{t}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X ,\]

since in every period the mass covers the distance \(4X\) (\(2X\) to the right and \(2X\) back) against a force of constant magnitude \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\). At \(X = 13{,}914\) mm this is the area \(0{,}1113\) J.

For a viscous damper with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) and the same motion, the loop is the ellipse with the same horizontal semi-axis \(X\), since the displacement is the same, and vertical semi-axis \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\), since \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\) and \(\dot q\) has amplitude \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) (at resonance \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)). Its area is \(\pi\,X\cdot c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) (the area of an ellipse with semi-axes \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\pi a b\), as used in figure 9.83). We choose \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) so that the areas agree: \(\pi\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi = 2{,}5465\) N. The vertical semi-axis of the ellipse is therefore \(2{,}5465\) N and exceeds \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N: the ellipse sticks out of the rectangle at \(q = 0\) and does not reach it at the corners, and the two loops enclose the same area. The direction of travel on the ellipse is the same as on the rectangle.

This is the rule that we introduce as a definition. The name has a reason: the damper is "equivalent" by what it removes (\(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period), and "viscous" because its force is proportional to the velocity, so the equation of motion stays linear. For a viscous damper the loss is \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\) by theorem 9.73, so we get \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) by setting this loss equal to the real one. In figure 20.11 this is the area of the loop, which stays the same when the rectangle is replaced by the ellipse.

Definition 20.6 Equivalent viscous damping (enakovredno viskozno dušenje)

Let \(q(t) = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) be a motion with amplitude \(X > 0\) and circular frequency \(\Omega > 0\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\), and let \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) be a piecewise continuous function of time with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) (the damping force in this motion). Let the energy lost in a period \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\), the area of the loop, be equation (20.4). The equivalent viscous damping coefficient is the number

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{W_{\mathrm{izg}}}{\pi\,\Omega\,X^2} \quad (\mathrm{N\,s/m}) \tag{20.5}\]

and the equivalent damping ratio is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}/(2\sqrt{km})\) (definition 9.5). A viscous damper with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) in the same motion loses exactly \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period.

Source: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 125 to 128): equation (4.75) (PDF p. 127) writes \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = -\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{D}}/(\pi\,\Omega\,U^2)\), where \(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{D}} = -W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the work of the damping force in a cycle and \(U\) is our \(X\). The equivalent damping ratio is in equations (4.76) to (4.78) (PDF p. 128). Our notation uses the letter \(q\) and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} > 0\) as in definition 20.1.

The number \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is not a property of the mechanism but of the mechanism in a given motion: it depends on \(X\) and in general on \(\Omega\). For an actual viscous damper (\(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\)) theorem 9.73 gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = c\) for every \(X\) and \(\Omega\), since then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\). Is equating the energies the only sensible choice, or could we take something else, say the same peak force? The answer is in the next theorem. We draw the friction force over a period (figure 20.12).

We label the horizontal axis with \(\theta = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), an angle that grows by \(2\pi\) in a period, and the displacement is \(q = X\sin\theta\) while its velocity is proportional to \(\cos\theta\). The dry friction force is piecewise constant: \(-F_{\mathrm{t}}\) while \(\cos\theta > 0\) (from \(0\) to \(\pi/2\) and from \(3\pi/2\) to \(2\pi\)), and \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\) in between, when the velocity is negative. The viscous force \(-c\,\dot q = -c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\theta\) is a cosine of amplitude \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\), the blue curve for the chosen \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). Which multiple of the velocity fits friction best? We measure the difference of the two forces, the remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q\), by the integral of its square over a period, \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q)^2\,\mathrm{d}t\), which is \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) times the mean square. We take the square because it does not depend on the sign of the deviation and squares are easy to work with (the proof below is a single completed square). We draw how this misfit changes with \(c\) for friction on cantilever \(A\) (figure 20.13).

On the horizontal axis we plot the coefficient \(c\) of a trial damper, on the vertical axis the misfit \(R(c)\). With no damper, at \(c = 0\), the remainder is the whole friction force, so there \(R(0) = F_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,T_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}7096\) N² s. As we increase \(c\), the cosine fits the step of friction better and better and the misfit falls until it reaches its lowest point at \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 5{,}167\) N s/m. What is left there is \(R(c_{\mathrm{eq}}) = 0{,}1344\) N² s, which is \(18{,}9\ \%\) of the starting value: no multiple of the velocity catches this part of the friction force. At a still larger \(c\) the viscous force is too large and the misfit grows again, by \(A\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2\) above the bottom with \(A = \pi\,\Omega X^2\). At \(c = 2c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) it is \(0{,}7096\) N² s again, as if there were no damper. And a damper with the same largest force as friction, \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = F_{\mathrm{t}}\)? It has \(c = 4{,}058\) N s/m and lies to the left of the vertex, with the misfit \(0{,}1609\) N² s. It fits worse and removes only \(\pi/4 = 78{,}5\ \%\) of the energy of friction in a period (the area \(\pi X F_{\mathrm{t}}\) of the ellipse against the area \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) of the rectangle), so with it we would compute too large an amplitude. The theorem says that the curve is a parabola with its vertex at \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) for every mechanism, not only for friction.

Theorem 20.7 The energy rule is the best viscous fit (pravilo energije je najboljši viskozni približek)

Let \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with \(X > 0\), \(\Omega > 0\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\) and let \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) be a piecewise continuous function with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\). For a real number \(c\) let (parabola of figure 20.13)

\[R(c) = \int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\bigl(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q\bigr)^2\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

Then:

  1. \(R(c) = R(c_{\mathrm{eq}}) + \pi\,\Omega X^2\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2\) with \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from definition 20.6. The function \(R\) therefore has exactly one minimum, at \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). In the figure this is the vertex of the parabola, and its bottom is \(R(c_{\mathrm{eq}})\).
  2. The remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\) is orthogonal to the velocity: \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\bigl(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\bigr)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). So the remainder does no work in a period. In figure 20.12 the remainder is the grey curve.
Proof

We must show that \(R\) is a quadratic function with leading coefficient \(\pi\,\Omega X^2\) and vertex at \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). In the figure these are the parabola and its vertex.

  1. We expand the square: \(R(c) = \int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t + 2c\int f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t + c^2\int \dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t\), all integrals over \([0, T_{\mathrm{p}}]\). The integrals exist because the integrands are piecewise continuous. They are numbers that do not depend on \(c\), so \(R\) is a quadratic function of the coefficient \(c\), and the first integral is its value at \(c = 0\).
  2. From \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we get \(\dot q = -\Omega X\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\) (theorem 8.13), and by lemma 9.72 (item 2 with \(a = -\varphi\)) \(\int\dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \Omega^2X^2\,T_{\mathrm{p}}/2 = \pi\,\Omega X^2\). This positive number stands in front of \(c^2\) and says how steeply the parabola opens.
  3. By equation (20.4), \(\int f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = -W_{\mathrm{izg}}\), and by equation (20.5) \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\pi\,\Omega X^2\). With \(A = \pi\,\Omega X^2 > 0\) we therefore have \(R(c) = \int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t - 2c\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}A + c^2A\). The term with \(c\) decides where the vertex lies.
  4. We complete the square: \(c^2A - 2c\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}A = A\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 - A\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}^2\), so \(R(c) = A\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 + \bigl(\int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t - A\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}^2\bigr)\). The binomial in the bracket does not contain \(c\) and equals \(R(c_{\mathrm{eq}})\) (insert \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\)), which is the height of the bottom. Since \(A > 0\) and \((c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 \ge 0\) with equality exactly at \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\), at the vertex, this is item 1.
  5. Item 2: \(\int(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\dot q)\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = -W_{\mathrm{izg}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\pi\,\Omega X^2 = 0\) by steps 2 and 3. The remainder is the grey curve of figure 20.12: its product with the velocity has equal positive and negative areas over a period.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (4.75) (PDF p. 127) gives the energy rule, not the property of the best fit.

The proof showed that the two rules are one and the same: whoever equates the energy lost in a period also finds the viscous force that is closest to the real one in the mean square. The reason is item 2: the remainder is orthogonal to the velocity, its work is zero, so the real force and the substitute do the same work in a period. We read figure 20.12 like this: the blue curve is the projection of the orange one onto the direction of the velocity (like the shadow of a vector on a line, hence the name "projection"), and the grey curve is what remains of the projection. For friction the square root of the mean square of the remainder is \(\sqrt{1 - 8/\pi^2} = 0{,}4352\) times the square root of the mean square of the friction force itself, that is \(43{,}5\ \%\). The number comes from item 2: since the remainder is orthogonal to the velocity, the mean square of the force splits into the mean square of the remainder and the mean square of the blue curve, as in Pythagoras' theorem. The friction force has mean square \(F_{\mathrm{t}}^2\), the blue cosine curve of amplitude \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi\) has \((4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi)^2/2 = 8F_{\mathrm{t}}^2/\pi^2\) (lemma 9.72), so \(F_{\mathrm{t}}^2(1 - 8/\pi^2)\) is left for the remainder. On the parabola the same ratio is the height of the bottom against the value at \(c = 0\): \(0{,}1344/0{,}7096 = 0{,}1894 = 0{,}4352^2\). As a force the remainder is therefore large, but in a harmonic motion it does not affect the energy in a period, and in describing the motion we neglect it. Section 20.2.2 shows what we neglect and how little it contributes.

The theorem holds for every mechanism. We test it on two that we already know: dry friction, and the quadratic drag of air or a liquid.

Corollary 20.8 Equivalent damping of dry friction (enakovredno dušenje suhega trenja)

For \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we have \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X\), the area of the rectangle, and

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{4F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,\Omega\,X} , \qquad \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{2F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,k\,X}\,\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{n}}}{\Omega} . \tag{20.6}\]
Proof

We must show the energy loss and from it \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). In figure 20.11 the loss is the area of the rectangle.

  1. Piece by piece, \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\,\dot q = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\), so \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = F_{\mathrm{t}}\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t\) by equation (20.4). The friction force is the step, which always points against the velocity, so its power is negative.
  2. \(|\dot q| = \Omega X\,|\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)|\) has period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\), so we may take the integral over \([0, T_{\mathrm{p}}]\) over \([\varphi/\Omega, \varphi/\Omega + T_{\mathrm{p}}]\) instead (lemma 9.108, item 3), where \(\Omega t - \varphi\) runs from \(0\) to \(2\pi\). The sine is nonnegative on the first half of this interval and nonpositive on the second, each half lasts \(T_{\mathrm{p}}/2\), and the integral of the magnitude of the sine over a half is \(2/\Omega\) (fundamental theorem 3.55, since \(\bigl(-\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)/\Omega\bigr)' = \sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\)). Hence \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t = \Omega X\cdot 2\cdot 2/\Omega = 4X\), which is exactly the path of the mass in a period, from \(-X\) to \(X\) and back. The path \(4X\) is twice the width of the rectangle \(2X\).
  3. \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), and by equation (20.5) \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X/(\pi\,\Omega X^2) = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi\,\Omega X)\). This is the area of the rectangle.
  4. \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}/(2m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\) (since \(\sqrt{km} = m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)) and \(m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = k\) give \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(2\pi\,m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\Omega X) = (2F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi\,k\,X))(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/\Omega)\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The loss \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) is the geometric work of friction on the path \(4X\), CK (3.45) to (3.50) (PDF p. 89) gives the equation of motion with friction.

For \(A\) at resonance and \(X = 13{,}914\) mm, \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4\cdot 2/(\pi\cdot 35{,}4175\cdot 0{,}013914) = 5{,}167\) N s/m, that is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}00146\). The viscous damping of system \(A\) is \(c = 35{,}418\) N s/m (\(\zeta = 0{,}01\)), so friction adds only about a seventh (\(14{,}6\ \%\) of the coefficient). We note that the \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) of friction falls with frequency and with amplitude. The loss \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) does not depend on the frequency at all and grows only in proportion to \(X\), while the loss \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\) of a viscous damper grows with \(\Omega\) and with \(X^2\), so at a larger \(\Omega\) or \(X\) the coefficient that gives the same loss must be smaller. We say the same with a picture, because it is the core of the concept: the equivalent damper is not one damper but a different one for every amplitude (figure 20.14).

On the left the axes are again the displacement \(q\) and the damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\). At the amplitude \(1\) mm the friction loop is a narrow rectangle, at \(5\) mm a wider one and at \(15{,}944\) mm the widest. All three have the same height, from \(-F_{\mathrm{t}}\) to \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\), because the friction force does not know the amplitude. For each we draw the ellipse of equal area: the first, the second and the third. In the equality of areas \(\pi\,X\,h = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) the amplitude cancels, so all three have the same vertical semi-axis, \(h = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi = 2{,}546\) N. But the vertical semi-axis of a viscous damper is \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\). For it to stay the same at every amplitude, \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = h/(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X)\) must fall as \(1/X\): at \(1\) mm it is \(71{,}90\) N s/m, at \(5\) mm \(14{,}38\) N s/m and at \(15{,}944\) mm \(4{,}51\) N s/m. The numbers above the loops are the loss factors \(\gamma = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi k X)\) of example 20.5 (definition 20.3), \(0{,}0406\), \(0{,}00812\) and \(0{,}00255\): the smaller the vibration, the larger the share of the stored energy that friction removes. On the right we plot the amplitude \(X\) horizontally and the vertical semi-axis \(h\) vertically. The equivalent damper of friction is the horizontal line at \(2{,}546\) N, the true viscous damper of cantilever \(A\) is the line \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\), which reaches \(20\) N at \(15{,}944\) mm. They cross at \(X = 2{,}03\) mm: in smaller vibrations friction does most of the damping, in larger ones viscosity.

On the left are the axes \(q\) and \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\). The quadratic drag force is small at low velocity and steep at high velocity, so the loop lies flat in the middle and rises steeply at the edges. We replace its area by the ellipse of equal area, as for friction. In the middle are the angle \(\theta = \Omega t - \varphi\) on the horizontal axis and \(|\sin\theta|^3\) on the vertical one, because the power of the drag is proportional to \(|\dot q|^3\). The curve has two equal humps, the first over \([0, \pi]\) and the second over \([\pi, 2\pi]\). On the right we plot the amplitude \(X\) and the coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\): for quadratic drag the line rises, for friction the hyperbola falls.

Corollary 20.9 Equivalent damping of quadratic drag (enakovredno dušenje kvadratnega upora)

For \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -a\,|\dot q|\,\dot q\) with \(a > 0\) (N s²/m²) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we have \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \tfrac{8}{3}\,a\,\Omega^2X^3\), the area of the loop, and

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{8}{3\pi}\,a\,\Omega\,X . \tag{20.7}\]
Proof

We must show the energy loss and from it \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). The loss is the area of the loop, and \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is the semi-axis of the ellipse with the same area.

  1. From \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q = -a\,|\dot q|^3\), equation (20.4) gives \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = a\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|^3\,\mathrm{d}t = a\,\Omega^3X^3\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)|^3\,\mathrm{d}t\). The integrand is the curve \(|\sin\theta|^3\).
  2. With \(\theta = \Omega t - \varphi\) the integral over a period is \((1/\Omega)\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin\theta|^3\,\mathrm{d}\theta = (2/\Omega)\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\) (the interval \([-\varphi, 2\pi - \varphi]\) is shifted to \([0, 2\pi]\) by lemma 9.108, item 3), since \(|\sin|\) is periodic with period \(\pi\) (lemma 8.11). Over a period there are two equal humps.
  3. Because \(\sin^3\theta = \sin\theta\,(1 - \cos^2\theta)\) we have \(\bigl(-\cos\theta + \tfrac13\cos^3\theta\bigr)' = \sin\theta - \cos^2\theta\sin\theta = \sin^3\theta\). By the fundamental theorem 3.55, \(\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \bigl(1 - \tfrac13\bigr) - \bigl(-1 + \tfrac13\bigr) = \tfrac43\). This is the area of one hump.
  4. So the integral over a period is \((2/\Omega)\cdot\tfrac43 = 8/(3\Omega)\) and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \tfrac83\,a\,\Omega^2X^3\). The area of both humps is twice that.
  5. By equation (20.5), \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \tfrac83\,a\,\Omega^2X^3/(\pi\,\Omega X^2) = \tfrac{8}{3\pi}\,a\,\Omega\,X\). This coefficient grows with \(X\) as a straight line.

Source: CK example 4.4 (PDF p. 127 to 128) treats the same drag and obtains \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 8\,a\,\Omega\,U/(3\pi)\) (p. 128, the numerator 8 stands in the text of the page). Steps 1 to 5 are ours.

A check with SymPy and NumPy: for \(a = 1\) N s²/m², \(X = 10\) mm and \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the numerical projection of theorem 20.7 gives \(0{,}300633\) N s/m, and formula (20.7) gives \(8\cdot 35{,}4175\cdot 0{,}01/(3\pi) = 0{,}300633\) N s/m as well. For friction the same check gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 5{,}1674\) N s/m from least squares and \(5{,}1674\) from formula (20.6). For quadratic drag \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) grows with the amplitude, for friction it falls: the first removes proportionally more energy at large displacements, the second at small ones. In figure 20.15 the straight line of the quadratic drag rises while the hyperbola of friction falls.

A real joint usually has several mechanisms at once: a viscous damper, friction in the connections, air drag. Must we compute each one separately, or can we add them into one number? The loops in figure 20.16 answer this.

The figure shows four loops of the same motion with the same scale on the axes: the ellipse of the viscous damper, the rectangle of friction, the loop of quadratic drag and, on the right, the loop of the sum of the forces, obtained by adding the heights of the first three at every displacement. Below is the stack: the areas of the first three loops, laid one on another, make exactly the area of the fourth.

Corollary 20.10 Sum of mechanisms (vsota mehanizmov)

Let \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = f_1 + f_2 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{N}}\) be a sum of piecewise continuous functions with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\). If \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the equivalent coefficient of the force \(f_{\mathrm{j}}\) in this motion (the loops of the individual forces), then

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N W_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N c_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N \zeta_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{20.8}\]
Proof

We must show that the energy is linear in \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\). The area of the sum loop is the sum of the areas of the individual loops.

  1. By equation (20.4), \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int(f_1 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{N}})\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\bigl(-\int f_{\mathrm{j}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\bigr) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{j}}\) by linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54). This is the stack: the areas add.
  2. Division by \(\pi\,\Omega X^2\) by equation (20.5) gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\), and division by \(2\sqrt{km}\) gives \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (§4.7, PDF p. 125 to 128) treats each mechanism separately.

The corollary holds for the same motion: we add the \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the same \(X\) and \(\Omega\). The sum is the number \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) that we use in the formulas of chapter 9. For \(A\) the viscous part is \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) and the friction adds \(0{,}00146\) at \(X = 13{,}914\) mm, so \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}01146\). At another amplitude the addition would be different, so the correct order is: first solve for \(X\) from the energy balance, then compute \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from it. The theorem below does this. In figure 20.16 we add the areas of the loops for the same motion.

20.2.1 Resonance with friction

We return to the opening question. At resonance, \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), a viscous system has the phase lag \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) by theorem 9.62 (\(\cos\varphi = 0\) because \(k - m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = 0\)), and so does the system with equivalent viscous damping, so \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and the force \(Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) is in phase with the velocity \(\dot q = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\). The exciting force therefore always points in the same direction as the velocity and supplies the largest possible energy in a period. How much is this, and when do friction and viscosity use it up? We draw the energies per period against the amplitude (figure 20.17).

On the horizontal axis we plot the amplitude \(X\) in mm, on the vertical axis the energy per period \(W\) in J. In a period the exciting force supplies \(\pi Q_0X\), this is the blackwhite line, which grows in proportion to the amplitude. Friction removes \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), the flat orange line, and the viscous damper \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}X^2\), the grey parabola. The sum of both losses we draw in blue. While the blue curve is below the blackwhite line, the system gains more in a period than it loses, and the amplitude grows. Where they cross, at \(13{,}914\) mm and \(0{,}8742\) J, the amplitude settles. Of this energy friction takes \(0{,}1113\) J and viscosity \(0{,}7629\) J. Without friction the grey parabola alone would catch the blackwhite line only at \(15{,}944\) mm. Friction alone catches it nowhere: the gap \((\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})\,X\) between the two lines only widens with the amplitude. The theorem says the same with a formula and with conditions.

Theorem 20.11 Resonance with dry friction (resonanca s trenjem)

Let a system with mass \(m > 0\) and spring \(k > 0\) (\(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\)) have a viscous coefficient \(c \ge 0\), friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\) and a force \(Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) (\(Q_0 > 0\)). Let \(T = 2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). In figure 20.17 these are the blackwhite line of supplied energy and the blue curve of the losses. Then:

  1. Every solution \(q\) with period \(T\) and a continuous velocity satisfies (equal areas)
    \[\int_0^T Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_0^T\bigl(c\,\dot q^2 + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
  2. For the trial motion \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) with \(X > 0\) (a harmonic approximation that does not solve the equation of motion exactly) the two sides of this equation evaluate to \(\pi\,Q_0\,X = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 + 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X\). For \(c > 0\) this equality (intersection) holds exactly for
    \[X = \frac{\pi\,Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}} , \tag{20.9}\]
    which requires \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} < \pi\,Q_0\).
  3. For \(c = 0\) and \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} \ne \pi\,Q_0\) the equality of item 2 holds for no \(X > 0\): no trial motion \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) satisfies the energy balance. The lines of supplied energy and of friction with different slopes meet only at the origin.
Proof

We must show first the energy balance over a period, then evaluate it for \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\). The balance is the equality of the areas of supplied and removed energy.

  1. We multiply the equation \(m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) = Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) by the velocity. As in lemma 9.71, \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t = Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q - c\,\dot q^2 - F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\), since \(\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\,\dot q = |\dot q|\). The terms on the right are the power supplied and the power lost.
  2. Because \(q\) is periodic with period \(T\), so is \(\dot q\), and hence \(\mathcal{E}(T) = \mathcal{E}(0)\). By the fundamental theorem 3.55, \(0 = \int_0^T \mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}t\), and this is item 1. This is the return of the energy to the same level.
  3. With \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) we have \(\dot q = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\). By lemma 9.72 (item 2 with \(a = 0\)), \(\int_0^T Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = Q_0\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\,T/2 = \pi\,Q_0X\), the line of the supplied energy, and \(\int_0^T c\,\dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2\), the parabola of the viscous loss. By step 2 of corollary 20.8, \(\int_0^T F_{\mathrm{t}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), the line of friction.
  4. Division by \(X > 0\) gives \(\pi\,Q_0 = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X + 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so equation (20.9), the crossing of the sum of the losses with the line of the supplied energy. Positivity of \(X\) requires \(\pi\,Q_0 > 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\) when \(c > 0\): the line of the supplied energy must be steeper than the line of friction.
  5. For \(c = 0\) the equation becomes \(\pi\,Q_0X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), that is \(\pi\,Q_0 = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\) after division by \(X \ne 0\). If this condition is violated, the equation has no solution \(X > 0\), which is item 3: two lines of different slopes cross only at the origin.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK treats resonance only with viscous damping (see theorem 9.66). The comparison with RK4 time stepping is in num-02.py.

For \(A\), \(\pi Q_0 = 62{,}832\) N and \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} = 8\) N, so \(X = (62{,}832 - 8)/(\pi\cdot 35{,}418\cdot 35{,}4175) = 13{,}914\) mm, the crossing in the figure. Viscous damping alone, \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), gives \(20/(35{,}418\cdot 35{,}4175) = 15{,}944\) mm as in chapter 9, the crossing of the grey parabola. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N, a tenth of the exciting force \(Q_0 = 20\) N, reduces the amplitude by \(12{,}7\ \%\). In terms of energy: in a period the force supplies \(\pi Q_0 X = \pi\cdot 20\cdot 0{,}013914 = 0{,}8742\) J, of which viscosity takes \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 0{,}7629\) J and friction \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X = 0{,}1113\) J, together \(0{,}8742\) J, equal to the energy supplied. We get the same with the replacement: the total coefficient is \(c + c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 35{,}418 + 5{,}167 = 40{,}585\) N s/m and the resonance formula of chapter 9, \(X = Q_0/(c_{\mathrm{total}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\), gives \(20/(40{,}585\cdot 35{,}4175) = 13{,}914\) mm.

The trial motion is not an exact solution: with it \(m\ddot q + k q = 0\), and the equation of motion would require \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t) = (Q_0 - c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), which fails for \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\) because the sign function is not a multiple of the cosine. The theorem therefore does not say whether the motion really settles at \(X = 13{,}914\) mm. We check this by time stepping (fourth-order Runge-Kutta, 200 steps per period, smoothed sign function, 400 periods, computed in num-02.py): the peak in period 400 is \(13{,}9138\) mm, the fundamental component \(13{,}9138\) mm and the energy formula \(13{,}9138\) mm, all agreeing to four decimals. Figure 20.18 shows how the amplitude settles.

On the horizontal axis we plot the number of periods \(n\), on the vertical axis the peak displacement \(X\). The system starts from rest, at \(n = 0\) we have \(X = 0\). Without damping, the dashed line, the peak grows by \(\pi Q_0/k = 1{,}0018\) mm per period, because the force supplies \(\pi Q_0 X\) in every period and \(\mathcal{E} = \tfrac12 kX^2\) (we derive the increment \(\pi Q_0/k\) two paragraphs below, with \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)). The grey curve, given by viscosity alone, is stopped by the damper at \(15{,}944\) mm, when the loss \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2\) reaches the energy supplied. The blue curve is damping with friction: it settles lower, at \(13{,}914\) mm, and has \(6{,}376\) mm after \(n = 10\) periods, \(9{,}893\) mm after \(20\), \(12{,}769\) mm after \(40\) and \(13{,}821\) mm after \(80\).

Why is there no settling with friction alone? This is the near miss of the theorem, item 3, and we see it in figure 20.17. Take \(c = 0\). At resonance with \(Q_0 = 20\) N and \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N the energy supplied is \(\pi Q_0X = 62{,}83\,X\) (J, \(X\) in m) and the loss of friction is \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X = 8\,X\). The difference \((\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})\,X = 54{,}83\,X\) is positive for every \(X\): the line of friction never catches up with the line of the supplied energy. The loss and the energy supplied are both proportional to \(X\), so their ratio does not depend on the amplitude and there is no \(X\) at which they would be equal. For a viscous damper or for quadratic drag the loss grows with a higher power of \(X\) (\(X^2\) or \(X^3\)), so the line of the energy supplied and the curve of the loss intersect at a finite \(X\).

How much does the amplitude grow in each period? The energy at a turning point is \(\tfrac12 k X^2\), and in a period it grows by approximately \((\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})\,\bar X\) with \(\bar X\) the mean peak in that period (we compute the energy supplied and the friction loss as if the motion in that period were harmonic with amplitude \(\bar X\)). From \(\tfrac12 k(X_{\mathrm{n}+1}^2 - X_{\mathrm{n}}^2) = \tfrac12 k\,(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}})(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} + X_{\mathrm{n}}) = k\,\bar X\,(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}})\) with \(\bar X = (X_{\mathrm{n}} + X_{\mathrm{n}+1})/2\) we get \(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}} \approx (\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})/k = 0{,}8742\) mm: the growth is a straight line, not an exponential curve. Time stepping confirms: after \(5\), \(10\) and \(20\) periods the peak is \(4{,}159\), \(8{,}530\) and \(17{,}272\) mm, with a mean increment from the fifth period on of \(0{,}8742\) mm per period (figure 20.18, the orange line). Without friction the increment would be \(1{,}0018\) mm. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N reduces the increment to \(0{,}8726\) of its former value but does not stop the growth. For \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > \pi Q_0/4 = 15{,}708\) N the loss would exceed the energy supplied at every amplitude and a harmonic motion could not last. What happens instead (the mass stops and starts again) the harmonic model does not say.

20.2.2 When the replacement is allowed

Replacing a damper by an equivalent viscous one rests on the assumption that the motion is harmonic. Theorem 20.7 tells us what we neglect: the remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\dot q\) of figure 20.12, the grey curve, has a root mean square of \(43{,}5\ \%\) of the root mean square of the friction force, and it consists of higher harmonic components. How large a deviation do they cause? The dry friction force \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\theta)\) has, by lemma 9.109 (orthogonality of the trigonometric system), an expansion in \(\cos n\theta\). The coefficient is \(a_{\mathrm{n}} = (1/\pi)\int_0^{2\pi}f_{\mathrm{D}}\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -(F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi)\int_0^{2\pi}\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\theta)\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). By the symmetries \(\theta \to -\theta\) and \(\theta \to \pi - \theta\) the integral is \(4\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 4\sin(n\pi/2)/n\) for odd \(n\), so \(a_1 = -4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi\) (this is exactly the blue \(-c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\theta\)) and \(a_3 = +4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(3\pi) = 0{,}8488\) N. The third-harmonic force with amplitude \(0{,}8488\) N drives the system at frequency \(3\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), where by theorem 9.62 the amplitude of the response is \(0{,}8488\,|H(3\omega_{\mathrm{n}})|\) with \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{(k - 9m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2)^2 + (3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}})^2}\). For \(A\), \(k - 9m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = -8k = -501\,760\) N/m and \(3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 3763\) N/m, so \(|H| = 1{,}993\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N and the response is \(1{,}69\cdot 10^{-3}\) mm, that is \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the amplitude \(X = 13{,}914\) mm. This deviation is almost exactly \(-1{,}69\cdot 10^{-3}\cos 3\theta\) mm (the phase shift is only \(3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(8k) = 0{,}0075\) rad), and at the peak of the fundamental component, at \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\cos 3\theta = 0\). The peak and the fundamental component therefore differ in time stepping by less than \(10^{-4}\) mm, and formula (20.9) gives the true amplitude to four decimals. The smallness has a reason: at resonance the system is not in resonance with the third harmonic, its response is \(1/8\) of the static one (\(8k\) in the denominator), and the friction force is already a small part of the excitation (\(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi = 2{,}5465\) N against \(Q_0 = 20\) N).

On the horizontal axis is the frequency \(\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), on the vertical one the logarithmic ratio of the response to the static one. With light damping the response has a narrow peak at \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), rising to \(1/(2\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}})\), about \(43\). The shaded band between \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 - \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}})\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}})\) is the half-power band, of width \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). At triple frequency the response is only \(1/8\) of the static one, more than three hundred times lower than the peak.

The replacement is therefore valid when three conditions hold:

  1. The motion is close to harmonic: the higher components of the damping force are small and the corresponding response smaller still. For \(A\) at resonance with friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}1\,Q_0\) this share is \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\). With larger friction or a weaker excitation, where the mass stops in between (sticks), the motion is no longer close to harmonic and the replacement fails. The remainder is the grey curve of figure 20.12, and its response at \(3\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) is barely visible.
  2. The damping is light, the ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is small (at resonance \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}0115\) for \(A\)). The resonance peak is then narrow, the half-power band is \(2\zeta\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) wide (theorem 9.74), and the system already filters the harmonic components outside this band. In figure 20.19 the band is shaded and the peak above it is tall.
  3. The replacement holds for one amplitude and one frequency: \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is a number at \(X\) and \(\Omega\), and if \(X\) changes, \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) changes too. Free vibration shows this last point. The height of the friction line in figure 20.14 is the same at every amplitude, so \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) changes with \(X\).

We draw the peaks of the free vibration of cantilever \(A\) with friction, vibration by vibration (figure 20.20).

On the horizontal axis we plot the number of vibrations \(n\), on the vertical axis the peak displacement \(X\) in mm, the mass starts at \(5\) mm. Free vibration with friction has a known answer: by theorem 9.150 the amplitude falls linearly, by \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/k = 0{,}12755\) mm per full vibration, so by \(1{,}2755\) mm in ten vibrations. The peaks lie on the orange line, and in example 9.151 the mass starting at \(5\) mm stops after \(39\) vibrations. What would we get if we computed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from the first vibration and used it as a fixed number? By equation (20.6) \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2u_{\mathrm{D}}/(\pi X)\) with \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = F_{\mathrm{t}}/k = 0{,}03189\) mm, at \(X = 5\) mm this is \(0{,}00406\). With it the decay would be exponential with a peak ratio \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}} = 0{,}9748\) per vibration, the blue curve, and after \(39\) vibrations the peak would still be \(5\cdot 0{,}3697 = 1{,}85\) mm (theorem 9.148), whereas the real motion stops, its peak at \(39\) vibrations is \(5 - 39\cdot 0{,}12755 = 0{,}025\) mm. Both values are the dots at \(n = 39\). The two curves agree at the start, because at \(5\) mm they have the same loss per vibration, and then they part. The reason: \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} \propto 1/X\) and so it grows as the amplitude falls. At \(X = 1\) mm it is \(0{,}0203\), at \(0{,}5\) mm \(0{,}0406\) and at \(0{,}1531\) mm \(0{,}1326\). The decrement that we measure between the last two peaks (\(0{,}2806\) and \(0{,}1531\) mm) gave \(\zeta = 0{,}0960\) in example 9.151, and this is close to the equivalent ratio at the middle of these two peaks, \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}(0{,}217\ \mathrm{mm}) = 0{,}094\) (figure 9.201). The number \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) of friction is therefore a reading at a single amplitude.

Summary: the damping force of any mechanism is replaced by a viscous one that removes the same energy in a period (definition 20.6). This is at the same time the best viscous fit in the mean square (theorem 20.7). So for resonance with friction (theorem 20.11) we obtained an amplitude that friction reduces by \(12{,}7\ \%\) without solving a nonlinear equation. The replacement holds for one amplitude and one frequency: for friction \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) falls as the amplitude or the frequency grows. Hysteretic damping, whose loss is by construction \(\pi\gamma kX^2\) and independent of frequency, is treated in section 20.3. The equality of the losses is clearest in the area of the loop, which the ellipse has equal to the friction rectangle.

20.3 Hysteretic damping

In section 20.1 we measured the loss in one period by the area of the loop of the damping force against displacement (figure 9.83), and in section 20.2 we replaced every mechanism by a viscous damper that loses the same energy. The viscous damper has a property that often fails in built structures: its loss in a period, \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), at the same amplitude \(X\) grows in proportion to the frequency \(\Omega\) (theorem 9.73). GR (§3.2.2, PDF p. 181, footnote 3) mentions structures with joints, where the mechanical joints cause dry friction and damping forces that do not grow linearly with frequency in harmonic motion. For such friction the reason is simple, and the rectangular loop of figure 20.11 shows it: the force is constant, \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the path covered in a period is \(4X\) (twice \(2X\), there and back), so the work is \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) however fast the motion goes. For cantilever \(A\) with \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N and \(X = 13{,}914\) mm this area is \(0{,}1113\) J at every frequency (computation in num-03.py). We ask whether there is a linear model of damping whose loss in a period does not depend on frequency.

From history

CK (§4.8, PDF p. 129) calls such damping structural and writes that it is often used in structural dynamics, for example in studies of aircraft vibration and flutter, and that Theodorsen and Garrick used it in an early study of flutter. CK introduces it with the notation of the complex frequency response of his section 4.3 and says that this notation is especially suitable for this damping.

Let us return to the question that opened the section. We draw the loop that the point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) runs through in a period, as before, for cantilever \(A\) at amplitude \(X = 15{,}944\) mm (figure 20.21). We hold the amplitude constant so that only the loops are compared, although the driving force would have to be adjusted at every frequency.

First the axes: displacement \(q\) horizontally, force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) vertically, on the horizontal axis the limit displacements \(-X\) and \(X\). The viscous damper of cantilever \(A\) (\(m = 50\) kg, \(k = 62\,720\) N/m) with \(\zeta = 0{,}01\), that is \(c = 2\zeta\sqrt{km} = 35{,}42\) N s/m, at resonance, \(r = 1\), gives an ellipse of height \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 20\) N and area \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 1{,}00\) J, which is the energy lost in a period (theorem 9.73).
