The same sum is given by the law of the material that we write in section 20.5.2, if we compute it for the stepwise strain piece by piece (in every piece the strain is constant, so the computation is an exponential function, and at a jump \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) stays continuous, since the dashpot does not move in an instant): \(0{,}903841\) in both computations (num-05.out).

The true stress (dashed line) at \(t = 3\tau\) is \(0{,}9804\), so with three steps the error is \(0{,}0765\), that is \(7{,}8\) %. Narrower steps do better, with the same computation (NumPy, steps at times \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = 3\tau i/N\)):

\(N\) step width \(\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}(3\tau)/(E_\infty\varepsilon_0)\) error
3 \(1\,\tau\) 0,903841 \(-7{,}81\) %
12 \(0{,}25\,\tau\) 0,984577 \(+0{,}43\) %
24 \(0{,}125\,\tau\) 0,983711 \(+0{,}34\) %
48 \(0{,}0625\,\tau\) 0,982328 \(+0{,}20\) %
96 \(0{,}03125\,\tau\) 0,981425 \(+0{,}11\) %
192 \(0{,}015625\,\tau\) 0,980923 \(+0{,}054\) %

For \(N \ge 24\) the error roughly halves with every doubling of \(N\) (the ratios of successive errors are \(0{,}58\), \(0{,}53\) and \(0{,}52\)), so for narrow steps it is roughly proportional to the step width \(h\). What is the sum when we narrow the steps? The step height is the difference of the values of a differentiable function at the ends of a piece of width \(h\), and by the mean value theorem \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \dot\varepsilon(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h\) for some point \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the piece. The sum is therefore like a Riemann sum

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) + \sum_{\mathrm{i} \ge 1} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\dot\varepsilon(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h ,\]

which has for its limit \(h \to 0\) the integral \(\int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) (the mark at the end of the integral only closes it, it is not a factor). This is an idea, not a proof: we do not know that the limit really is the stress of the model, and for a general linear material it is the Boltzmann principle, which we cite without proof (CM, equations (9.3.7)-(9.3.9), PDF p. 438, BOWER, PDF p. 137). A proof for the models that the section treats we get as with the Duhamel integral: we write the formula as a candidate and check that it solves the equations of the model.

20.5.2 Prony material

Which models have equations that we can check? The standard linear solid of section 20.4 is a spring \(E_\infty\) in parallel with one Maxwell element (definition 20.22). Why not more elements? BOWER says that simple models are too far from the measurements of a polymer over a longer time, and so he connects in parallel several Maxwell elements, each with its own time, and a spring in parallel with all of them (BOWER, PDF p. 139). The text layer of the book on this page says that the elements are connected "in series", but the formula for \(G(t)\) is the relaxation modulus of a parallel connection (a misprint of the book, PDF p. 139): at a common strain the stresses add, in a series connection the compliances would add. We take the parallel connection: lemma 20.29 below shows that it gives exactly Bower's formula.

We write the law of one Maxwell element with the strain of the dashpot, so that the equation has no derivative of the strain \(\varepsilon\), since at a jump it does not exist. Let us draw the bar as in figure 20.43 at the top. The left end is held by a wall, the right end is a plate that is here before the stretch and here after it. We draw the bar with unit length, so the displacement of the plate is the strain \(\varepsilon\) itself. Between the wall and the plate there are in parallel the spring \(E_\infty\), the Maxwell element \(j\) and more such elements. A Maxwell element is a spring of stiffness \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) in series with a dashpot in which the stress is proportional to the rate of its strain, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}} = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the coefficient \(\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the stress in element \(j\). Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\) be the strain of the dashpot: the joint between the dashpot and the spring moves by this much. The spring therefore stretches only by the rest, \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\): the dashed line shows where its right end would be if the spring only moved with the joint and did not stretch. Both elements carry the same stress (series connection: only the spring and the dashpot act on the joint, the joint has no mass, so by Newton's second law their forces are equal and opposite): \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}) = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\). With \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}/E_{\mathrm{j}}\) we get \(\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = (\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). At time zero the dashpot has not yet moved, \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0\): at a finite stress its rate \(\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}/\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\) is finite, and a finite rate covers no distance in zero time. This is the assumption of rest from the opening of the section. When it does not hold and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = a_{\mathrm{j}} \ne 0\) (the bar was deformed before), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) differs by \(a_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\), because the difference of two solutions of the same equation solves \(\dot y = -y/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). The stress is then smaller by \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\), and at \(t = 3\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) there is \(\mathrm{e}^{-3}\) of this correction left, that is \(5\) %. The stresses of the rows add because all of them pull the same plate: on it act the spring \(E_\infty\) with the stress \(E_\infty\varepsilon\) and every element with its own \(E_{\mathrm{j}}(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})\), and the massless plate is at rest only if the external stress \(\sigma\) balances them. We call the time \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) the relaxation time (relaksacijski čas) of element \(j\): it has the unit second and tells in what time, after a step, the strain of the spring \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) decreases by a factor \(\mathrm{e}\) (which lemma 20.29 proves).

Definition 20.28 Prony series and Prony material (Pronyjeva vrsta in Pronyjev material)

Let \(N \ge 1\) be an integer, \(E_\infty \ge 0\) and \(E_1, \dots, E_{\mathrm{N}} > 0\) moduli in pascals, and \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_{\mathrm{N}} > 0\) times in seconds. The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} : [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.18}\]

is a Prony series (Pronyjeva vrsta). Let \(T > 0\) and \(\varepsilon : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous function (the strain after time zero, the value \(\varepsilon(0)\) is the strain right after the start, before time zero the strain is zero). A Prony material (Pronyjev material) has the stress

\[\sigma(t) = E_\infty\,\varepsilon(t) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\big(\varepsilon(t) - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\big) , \tag{20.19}\]

where the internal variables (notranje spremenljivke) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) are solutions of the equations

\[\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \frac{\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0 \qquad (j = 1, \dots, N) . \tag{20.20}\]

Since \(\varepsilon\) is continuous, each equation has by lemma 9.39 (with \(s = -1/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(f = \varepsilon/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\)) exactly one solution, which is differentiable everywhere, so \(\sigma\) is thereby a uniquely determined continuous function.

Source: A series of exponential terms and a spring in parallel with the Maxwell elements are BOWER, PDF p. 139 ("Prony series", the text says "in series", see above). The notation with the strain of the dashpot as an internal variable is ours. We quote the name "Prony" as BOWER uses it, we have not read the reason for it.

For \(N = 1\) and \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\) the Prony series has the same \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) as the standard linear solid. We check that this function really is the response to a step.

Lemma 20.29 Relaxation modulus of a Prony material (relaksacijski modul Pronyjevega materiala)

Let a Prony material have the strain \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\) for every \(t \in [0, T]\) (a step at time zero). Then \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t) = \varepsilon_0\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) and \(\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\) with \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) from equation (20.18). The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is positive and strictly decreasing, \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}} =: E_0\) and \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) \to E_\infty\) for \(t \to \infty\).

Proof

We must show that the announced \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) solves equation (20.20), then compute the sum (20.19).

  1. The function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t) = \varepsilon_0\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) (the blackwhite curve) has \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0\) and \(\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). On the other hand \((\varepsilon_0 - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). The function solves equation (20.20), and by uniqueness (lemma 9.39) it is \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. We insert into equation (20.19): \(\varepsilon_0 - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) (the blue curve, the stretch of the spring), so \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0\,\big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\).
  3. All terms \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) are positive and \(E_\infty \ge 0\), so \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} > 0\). The derivative \(\dot E_{\mathrm{rel}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} < 0\), so it is strictly decreasing. At \(t = 0\) we have \(\mathrm{e}^0 = 1\). Since the exponential function with a negative argument decreases toward zero, the limit is \(E_\infty\).

Source: The formula is BOWER, PDF p. 139. CM, PDF p. 438, demands of the relaxation modulus non-negativity, monotone decrease and a finite limit, which we prove here for the series (20.18). The proof is ours.

The steps of the proof are shown in the bottom part of figure 20.43. On the axes are the time in units of \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and the strain in units of \(\varepsilon_0\). At the step only the spring stretches in an instant, the dashpot is still at zero. Then the strain of the dashpot grows toward the value \(\varepsilon_0\), because the spring pulls it, and so the stretch of the spring, the difference between the dashed line and the blackwhite curve, falls. With it falls the stress of the element. At \(t = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) there is \(\mathrm{e}^{-1} = 0{,}3679\) of the stretch left.

The lemma tells two things that we use. First, \(E_0\) is the modulus right after a step, \(E_\infty\) the modulus after a long time. This suggests that a bar is stiffer when we load it faster, which is the promise of the section on linear elasticity for polymers such as nylon (BOWER, PDF pp. 96, 120). The example in section 20.5.6 shows it with a number. Second, \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) really is the time in which the stress of element \(j\), \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\varepsilon_0\), falls by a factor \(\mathrm{e}\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{-\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} = \mathrm{e}^{-1}\).

20.5.3 Hereditary integral

Now we have everything to prove the idea of figure 20.42. We insert the candidate that the idea announces into the equations (20.20) and check that it satisfies them. For this we need the derivative of an integral in which \(t\) appears both in the upper limit and in the integrand (lemma 9.94 from chapter 9), and the theorem on uniqueness of the solution of a first-order equation (lemma 9.39). The strain may be piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), which covers a ramp that stops after time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\), and a jump in the rate.

Theorem 20.30 Hereditary integral (dedni integral)

Let the material be a Prony material (definition 20.28) with relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\), \(T > 0\) and \(\varepsilon : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous function that is piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), with a piecewise continuous derivative \(\dot\varepsilon\). Then the stress (20.19) for every \(t \in [0, T]\) is

\[\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{20.21}\]
Proof

We must show that every term of the sum (20.19) has the form (20.21). The term with \(E_\infty\) is the fundamental theorem of calculus. For the term with index \(j\) we take the candidate \(R_{\mathrm{j}}\) that the idea announces, and show that it has the same equation and the same initial value as \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. Let \(E_\infty \ge 0\). By lemma 6.12 (a continuous piecewise continuously differentiable function) \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), so \(E_\infty\,\varepsilon(t) = E_\infty\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t E_\infty\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. Let \(j\) be fixed and \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). Let \(R(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\varepsilon(0) + G(t)\) with \(G(t) = \int_0^t \mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau}\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The kernel \(g(t, s) = \mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau}\) is continuous on the square \([0, T]^2\), differentiable in \(t\) with the derivative \(\partial g/\partial t = -g/\tau\), which is continuous, and \(g(t, t) = 1\). The candidate says what the idea predicts: every change of strain at time \(s\) stretches the spring of the element, and this stretch decays until time \(t\) by the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau}\), like the blue curve.
  3. By lemma 9.94 \(G\) is continuous and at every point \(t\) that is not a division point of \(\dot\varepsilon\) differentiable with the derivative \(G'(t) = g(t, t)\,\dot\varepsilon(t) + \int_0^t (-g(t, s)/\tau)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \dot\varepsilon(t) - G(t)/\tau\) (the increment comes from the new step, the decay of the stretch reduces it). The derivative of the first term of \(R\) is \(-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\varepsilon(0)/\tau\). So \(R\) is continuous, \(R(0) = \varepsilon(0)\) and at these points \(\dot R = \dot\varepsilon - R/\tau\). The derivative is piecewise continuous.
  4. Let \(D = \varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\), that is the stretch of the spring of the element. The function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuously differentiable (lemma 9.39, \(f = \varepsilon/\tau\) continuous), so \(D\) is continuous and \(D(0) = \varepsilon(0) - 0\). At the same points as in step 3 we have \(\dot D = \dot\varepsilon - (\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau = \dot\varepsilon - D/\tau\).
  5. Let \(W = D - R\), the difference of the spring stretch and the candidate. It is continuous, \(W(0) = 0\) and at every point outside finitely many division points \(\dot W = -W/\tau\), that is \(\dot W - sW = 0\) for \(s = -1/\tau\). By uniqueness in lemma 9.39 (\(f = 0\), \(y_0 = 0\)) \(W = 0\), so \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = R\).
  6. We multiply step 5 by \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) and add over \(j\) together with step 1, because all rows pull the same plate. By linearity of the integral (lemma 6.10, point 2) \(\sigma(t) = \big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t \big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), and this is equation (20.21).

Source: The formula is CM, equations (9.3.7)-(9.3.8), PDF p. 438, and BOWER, PDF p. 137, for an arbitrary linear material (Boltzmann superposition principle, not proved there and not here either). The proof for a Prony material by verification and first-order uniqueness is not from the source, it is the same as the path of the proof of theorem 9.96.

What did the theorem show and what not? It showed that for a Prony material the stress at time \(t\) is the integral of the strain rate \(\dot\varepsilon(s)\) multiplied by the weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\), and that the jump at the start contributes its own term. It did not show that the same holds for an arbitrary linear material (this is the Boltzmann principle, which we cite), nor for a history with jumps later than at time zero: then the expression gets a further term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) for every jump (as in figure 20.42, but we do not prove this here. CM, PDF p. 438, equation (9.3.6), writes the initial jump together with the integral as a Stieltjes integral, for the creep compliance). The weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\) tells with what modulus a change of strain at time \(s\) still contributes to the stress at time \(t\). Since \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) decreases (lemma 20.29), older changes count less than newer ones.

We test the theorem on the same example as in figure 20.42, now for \(t = 3\tau\). We draw the axis \(s\) and on it the strain rate \(\dot\varepsilon(s)/\varepsilon_0 = \cos(2s/\tau)\), which is positive at the start, negative from \(0{,}79\,\tau\) to \(2{,}36\,\tau\) and again positive. Across it we draw the weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau - s)\): at \(s = 0\) it is \(1{,}0498\), because \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau) = E_\infty(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3})\), and at \(s = t\), where the integral ends, it is \(2\), because \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_0\). Below is the product of the two. Its signed area is \(\int_0^{3\tau}E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = -0{,}0694\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\): the positive parts (\(s < 0{,}79\,\tau\) and \(s > 2{,}36\,\tau\)) have the areas \(0{,}5337\) and \(0{,}6507\), the negative part \(-1{,}2538\), and the sum is negative. The newer positive part counts more than the older one although it is narrower, because the weight beside it is larger. We add the jump \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) = 1{,}0498\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), and get \(\sigma(3\tau) = 0{,}9804\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The same follows from the law with the internal variable if we solve equation (20.20) with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (4000 steps): \(0{,}980390\), the difference from the integral is \(4 \cdot 10^{-14}\). The data are in num-05.out.

20.5.4 An example that fails the test: without the jump

We could regard the term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0)\) in the theorem as unnecessary, since the integral holds all the strain rate. Let us test this. We try the simplest history, the step \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0\) for all \(s \in [0, T]\), which is continuous and has \(\dot\varepsilon = 0\). The formula with only the integral would give \(\sigma(t) = \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\cdot 0\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). A bar that we stretched at time zero and hold would have no stress. But lemma 20.29 says that the stress is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\), that is \(1{,}6065\), \(1{,}3679\) and \(1{,}1353\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) at \(t = 0{,}5\tau\), \(\tau\) and \(2\tau\) (model D, the curve of the standard linear solid). The difference is all of the stress. The reason is that the whole jump from zero to \(\varepsilon_0\) at time zero is collected in the value \(\varepsilon(0)\): the history on \([0, T]\) is a constant and its derivative is zero everywhere, and the jump before the start the integral \(\int_0^t\dot\varepsilon\) does not see. Theorem 20.30 says this with the term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0)\) and in the case \(\varepsilon \equiv \varepsilon_0\) the whole answer is this term. In figure 20.42 it is the same: the jump \(\Delta_0\) gives the first term of the sum, and without it the sum at \(3\tau\) would be \(-0{,}1459\) instead of \(0{,}9038\).

A second example that fails the test is the Kelvin-Voigt element: a spring and a dashpot in parallel between a wall and a plate have no relaxation modulus as a function. If we stretch it in an instant, the dashpot would have to cover the finite elongation in an instant, the rate would be infinite and so would the stress in the dashpot. This is why BOWER says that the Kelvin-Voigt model has no well-defined relaxation modulus (BOWER, PDF p. 138). Such an element is not a Prony material and theorem 20.30 does not hold for it. Its response to a stress history is computed by CM from the compliance (CM, example 9.3.1, PDF p. 439), the reverse question, which we do not treat here.

20.5.5 Memory in \(N\) numbers

Formula (20.21) demands the whole history: in the sum of steps we must store all steps and at every time step multiply them all by a new weight, so there is more work with every step. A Prony material, however, has a short memory: the strain history influences the stress only through \(N\) numbers \(\alpha_1(t), \dots, \alpha_{\mathrm{N}}(t)\). Let us show this on one time step.

On the axes are the time \(u\) from \(0\) to \(h\) and the strain. The strain \(\varepsilon\) on the piece is a line with slope \(r\). The internal variable at the start of the piece is \(a = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}})\), the number that the whole past has brought. The curve \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) runs toward a line that lies \(r\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) below \(\varepsilon\) (the lag), because the junction, and the dashpot with it, lags behind the plate by as much as the spring stretch \(r\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) needs to drive the dashpot at the rate \(r\). The end of the piece gives \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}+1})\), the only number that we need for the next step.

Lemma 20.31 Update of the internal variables (posodobitev notranjih spremenljivk)

Let the material be a Prony material, \(0 \le t_{\mathrm{n}} < t_{\mathrm{n}+1} \le T\), \(h = t_{\mathrm{n}+1} - t_{\mathrm{n}}\), and let \(\varepsilon\) be linear on \([t_{\mathrm{n}}, t_{\mathrm{n}+1}]\), \(\varepsilon(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,u\) with \(r = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}})/h\). Then for every \(j\) the value at the end of the piece

\[\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1} - r\,\tau_{\mathrm{j}} + \big(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}}) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,\mathrm{e}^{-h/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.22}\]

and the stress at \(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) is equation (20.19) with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) and the \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}+1})\) so obtained. The history before \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\) influences the stress at \(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) only through the \(N\) numbers \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}})\).

Proof

We must show that the expression in \(u\) solves equation (20.20) on the piece and has the right initial value, then use uniqueness.

  1. Let \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(a = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \(y(u) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,u - r\,\tau + (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}\) for \(u \in [0, h]\). Then \(y(0) = a\) and \(y'(u) = r - (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}/\tau\).
  2. On the other hand \((\varepsilon(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) - y(u))/\tau\) \(= \big(r\,\tau - (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}\big)/\tau\), which is exactly the same as \(y'(u)\).
  3. The function \(u \mapsto \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u)\) solves the same equation with the same initial value \(a\) (the coefficients do not depend on time, chain rule, as in step 10 of the proof of theorem 9.96). By uniqueness (lemma 9.39, with a shift of time) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) = y(u)\). At \(u = h\) this is equation (20.22).

Source: The proof is not from a source, it is derived from lemma 9.39.

A test. Let us take the history of figure 20.44, but now piece by piece linear between the values \(\varepsilon(s_{\mathrm{n}})\) at steps \(h = 0{,}5\tau\), from \(0\) to \(3\tau\). Six updates by equation (20.22) give \(\sigma(3\tau) = 0{,}9625824501\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), and the hereditary integral of the same piecewise linear history gives \(0{,}9625824501\), the difference is in computer precision. Let us compare also with a simpler route. If we solve equation (20.20) with the explicit Euler method with the same step, \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} \leftarrow \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} + h\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), we get \(1{,}0202\), \(6\) % too much. The reason is the memory factor, which figure 20.43 shows at the bottom: instead of the curve Euler takes its tangent at the start, so at \(h = 0{,}5\,\tau\) instead of \(\mathrm{e}^{-h/\tau} = 0{,}6065\) it takes \(1 - h/\tau = 0{,}5\) (the difference \(0{,}1065\), for \(\tau = \tau_1\)), so the bar forgets too fast, because the step \(0{,}5\,\tau\) is not small against the relaxation time. Equation (20.22) has the exponent exactly. The comparison is not a proof, it only shows that a crude difference scheme must not be used when the step is comparable to the relaxation time.

20.5.6 Example: loading rate

The promise of the section on the linearly elastic material, that the behaviour of polymers depends on the loading rate, we now fulfil with a number. We stretch the bar uniformly to \(\varepsilon_0\) in the time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\): \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0 s/t_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(s \le t_{\mathrm{r}}\), so \(\varepsilon(0) = 0\) and \(\dot\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0/t_{\mathrm{r}}\). There is no jump and theorem 20.30 gives

\[\sigma(t_{\mathrm{r}}) = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{r}}} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t_{\mathrm{r}} - s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \varepsilon_0\Big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\Big) ,\]

since \(\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\mathrm{e}^{-(t_{\mathrm{r}}-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) (lemma 9.95, point 1). For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\) we have \((\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}})(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}) \to 1\) (the derivative of the function \(x \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-x}\) at \(x = 0\) is \(-1\), so \((1 - \mathrm{e}^{-x})/x \to 1\) for \(x \to 0\), here with \(x = t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\)), the stress is \(E_0\,\varepsilon_0\) as for a step. For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to \infty\) we have \((\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}})(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}) \le \tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\), and the stress is \(E_\infty\,\varepsilon_0\).

In the figure there is the axis \(t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau\) in logarithmic form, the limits \(E_0\) and \(E_\infty\) as dashed lines and the curve between them. For model D the stress at the end for three ramps is \(1{,}9516\), \(1{,}6321\) and \(1{,}1000\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), when \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) equals \(0{,}1\,\tau\), \(\tau\) and \(10\,\tau\). The same strain gives, if we reach it in a tenth of the relaxation time, \(1{,}77\) times as much stress (\(1{,}95\)) as if we reach it in ten times the relaxation time (\(1{,}10\)). At \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = \tau\) the formula gives \(1 + 1\cdot(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-1}) = 1{,}6321\), which is a point on the curve. The modulus of a polymer is therefore undetermined without the stated loading rate.

20.5.7 What follows

A strain history that is not a step demands weights. For a material whose relaxation modulus is a sum of exponential terms the hereditary integral (20.21) is exact (theorem 20.30), not only an approximation by steps. The memory of the material is in \(N\) internal variables (lemma 20.31). What the integral gives for an oscillating strain is shown in section 20.6: it takes \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega s\) and computes the phase of the stress against the strain. Sources of the section: CM §9.3.1 (PDF pp. 436-439), BOWER §3.6.2 (PDF pp. 136-137) and §3.6.4 (PDF p. 139). The paths of the proofs (verification and uniqueness) are from theorem 9.96, the numbers are in outlines/ch-dusenje/num-05.out.

20.6 Complex modulus and loss factor of a material

In section 20.3 we wrote the stiffness for steady vibration as \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) with a constant loss factor \(\gamma\), but that was not a model in time: one root of the characteristic polynomial had a positive real part, so the solution grew in time (lemma 20.18). In sections 20.4 and 20.5 we looked at a material with memory, in which the stress follows from the whole past history of the deformation. Now we join the two routes. What does such a material do when we stretch and compress it steadily with frequency \(\Omega\), as a vibrating structure does? How much energy does it lose in one period, and what does that depend on? Do we really get the constant \(\gamma\) of section 20.3 from its model, and on what band of frequencies does it hold (figure 20.55)?

The model is this. We watch a point of the material in a uniaxial stress state: the stress \(\sigma(t)\) and the strain \(\varepsilon(t)\) are numbers, tied together by the relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\) of definition 20.20. The material is linearly viscoelastic (definition 20.19), and its relaxation modulus is a Prony series (definition 20.28),

\[E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad E_\infty \ge 0 ,\ E_{\mathrm{j}} > 0 ,\ \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0 , \tag{20.23}\]

with finitely many terms. Each term is the relaxation of one branch made of a spring \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) and a dashpot \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) in series (a Maxwell element, definition 20.22), and \(E_\infty\) is a spring that does not give way. The sum \(E_0 = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the initial modulus. The standard linear solid of section 20.4 is the case \(N = 1\) with \(E_\infty > 0\). The symbol \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) here is a relaxation time, as in section 20.4, and has nothing to do with shear stress. Linearity is the assumption we need here: twice the strain gives twice the stress. Because of it the number we are looking for will not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\) and the loop will be an ellipse. It holds as long as the material fits definition 20.19, which is at small strains. Where it no longer fits, the loop is not an ellipse and one number per frequency is not enough. We impose the strain from \(t = 0\) on, \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\) for \(t \ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon(t) = 0\) before, with real \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\Omega > 0\). At \(t = 0\) there is a jump \(\varepsilon_0\), for which the hereditary integral has its own term (theorem 20.30). We will draw the response as a loop of stress against strain (figure 20.49).

We will write the answer with one complex number. The expression for the stress will have two parts: a vibration with frequency \(\Omega\) that does not end, and terms that die out with \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\). The first gets a name (its loop is shown in figure 20.49).

Definition 20.32 Complex modulus (kompleksni modul)

Let a material under the strain \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) (the loop is shown in figure 20.49), after the transient terms that tend to zero have died out, give the stress

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\hat E(\Omega)\,\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) \tag{20.24}\]

with a complex number \(\hat E(\Omega)\) that does not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(t\). The number \(\hat E(\Omega) = E_{\mathrm{shr}}(\Omega) + \mathrm{i}\,E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega)\) is the complex modulus (kompleksni modul) at frequency \(\Omega\), its real part \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is the storage modulus (shranjevalni modul), its imaginary part \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the loss modulus (izgubni modul), and the quotient

\[\gamma(\Omega) = \frac{E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega)}{E_{\mathrm{shr}}(\Omega)} \qquad (E_{\mathrm{shr}} > 0) \tag{20.25}\]

is the loss factor of the material (faktor izgub materiala). If for \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\) we write the stress as \(\sigma(t) = \sigma_0\cos(\Omega t + \delta)\) with amplitude \(\sigma_0 > 0\) and a phase shift \(\delta\) by which the stress leads the strain, then \(\hat E = (\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\delta}\), so \(\gamma = \tan\delta\).

Explanation

The names have a reason. The modulus is "complex" because it is a number with a real and an imaginary part. The part in phase with the strain, \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), acts like a spring: the loss in a period does not contain it (lemma 20.34). The part that leads the strain by a quarter of a period, \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), loses energy. The hat over \(E\) separates the modulus from \(E^*\) of chapter 11, which is the plane-strain modulus, and the primes of the sources (\(E'\), \(E''\)) mean a derivative, so we do not use them. Compare with \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) of section 20.3: there \(\gamma\) is constant, here it is a function of frequency, as the lower curve of figure 20.51 shows.

Source: GR equations (3.32) and (3.33) (PDF p. 181) write \(E_{\mathrm{hysteretic}} = E' + \mathrm{i}E''\) and \(E'(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) with "storage modulus", "loss modulus" and "loss factor" \(E''/E'\). BOWER section 3.6.1.2 (PDF p. 134) introduces the same for the shear modulus, \(G^* = \tau_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\delta}/2\varepsilon_0 = G' + \mathrm{i}G''\) (the factor 2 comes from the tensor shear strain, \(G = \tau/2\varepsilon\) on PDF p. 132). The same page prints \(G' = \tau_0\cos\delta/\varepsilon_0\) and \(G'' = \tau_0\sin\delta/\varepsilon_0\) without the factor 2. This is a misprint, since the real and imaginary parts of \(G^*\) are \(\tau_0\cos\delta/2\varepsilon_0\) and \(\tau_0\sin\delta/2\varepsilon_0\). Here is the uniaxial form, and the symbols \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) are the book's choice.

Does the number of the definition exist, and how large is it? For a Prony series we compute it from the hereditary integral of section 20.5, and we draw the result in figure 20.51.

Theorem 20.33 Complex modulus of a Prony series (kompleksni modul Pronyjeve vrste)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus (20.23) and let \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\) for \(t \ge 0\) and \(0\) before, \(\varepsilon_0, \Omega > 0\). Then for \(t > 0\)

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\hat E(\Omega)\,\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N}\frac{E_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.26}\]

where

\[\hat E(\Omega) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{\mathrm{i}\,\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} . \tag{20.27}\]

So the material has the complex modulus (20.27) (curves: figure 20.51), and

\[E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\frac{\Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2} , \qquad E_{\mathrm{izg}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\frac{\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2} . \tag{20.28}\]
Idea

We write the hereditary integral of section 20.5 for the complex strain \(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), because the exponential function integrates as in the real case. Each term of the series gives two parts: a vibration with frequency \(\Omega\) and a remainder \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\). We take the real part at the end, and we see the loop it traces in figure 20.49.

Proof

We must show the form (20.26). We write the stress with the hereditary integral, insert the series and integrate each term with the fundamental theorem.

  1. For \(t \ge 0\) we have \(\varepsilon(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) and \(\varepsilon(0+) = \varepsilon_0\). The derivative of the complex exponential function is \((\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s})' = \mathrm{i}\Omega\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\) (theorem 9.34, item 3), so \(\dot\varepsilon(s) = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}) = -\Omega\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega s\) (definition 9.33). By theorem 20.30
    \[\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0 + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  2. The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is real, and the integral of a complex function is the integral of its real part plus \(\mathrm{i}\) times the integral of its imaginary part, so \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\,Z\) for
    \[Z(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0 + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  3. After inserting the series (20.23) we have \(Z = Z_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Z_{\mathrm{j}}\). The term with \(E_\infty\) is \(Z_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\big(1 + \int_0^t\mathrm{i}\Omega\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55) and step 1 the integral is \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - 1\), so \(Z_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\).
  4. For term \(j\) we have \(Z_{\mathrm{j}} = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} + E_{\mathrm{j}}\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\,I_{\mathrm{j}}\) with \(I_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s\). Let \(\lambda = 1/\tau_{\mathrm{j}} + \mathrm{i}\Omega \ne 0\). By theorem 9.34, item 1, the integrand is \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}\), and the antiderivative is \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}/\lambda\) by item 3. The fundamental theorem gives \(I_{\mathrm{j}} = (\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})/\lambda\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t} = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), and \(1/\lambda = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\).
  5. Therefore
    \[Z_{\mathrm{j}} = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\Big[\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\Big] = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\Big[\frac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\Big] ,\]
    because \(1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\).
  6. The sum is \(Z = \hat E\,\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\) with \(\hat E\) from (20.27). Since \(1/(1 + \mathrm{i}y) = (1 - \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2)\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) is real, the real part of the second term equals the term in (20.26). This is the difference between the curves in the figure after the theorem.
  7. For the split of \(\hat E\) we use \(\mathrm{i}y/(1 + \mathrm{i}y) = \mathrm{i}y(1 - \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2) = (y^2 + \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2)\) with \(y = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). This gives (20.28). The transient terms are \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) and tend to zero (from \(5\tau\) on the figure no longer shows them), and the number \(\hat E\) does not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(t\), so definition 20.32 holds.
Explanation

The remainder is not small at once. After the time \(5\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) (vertical line) we have \(\mathrm{e}^{-5} = 0{,}0067\), so below \(0{,}7\ \%\) of the original value of term \(j\), and the "steady" state makes sense only from there on. The core of the theorem is that all terms of the forced part, \(E_\infty\) and \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\), are multipliers of the same \(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). The jump at \(t = 0\) affects only the remainder: at \(t = 0\) we get \(\sigma(0+) = \mathrm{Re}\hat E\varepsilon_0 + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2) = \varepsilon_0(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}) = E_0\varepsilon_0\) (orange point), as it must be for a jump of strain (initial modulus \(E_0\)). The loop of the steady part is shown in figure 20.49.

Source: The theorem is proved from the hereditary integral for Prony series, which theorem 20.30 provides. BOWER section 3.6.1.2 (PDF p. 134) only states the complex modulus. The proof is not from the source.

Let us draw the response of the theorem for a standard linear solid with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) and \(\Omega\tau = 1\). Here \(\hat E = (1{,}5 + 0{,}5\,\mathrm{i})\,E_\infty\), and the remainder is \(0{,}5\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) (figure 20.48).

On the axes are time in units of \(\tau\) and stress in units of \(E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The grey dashed curve is the steady part \(\mathrm{Re}(\hat E\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\), which starts at \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0 = 1{,}5\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) and oscillates with the amplitude \(|\hat E|\varepsilon_0 = 1{,}5811\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The orange curve is the whole stress. It starts at the point \(E_0\varepsilon_0 = 2\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), \(0{,}5\) above the steady part: this is the remainder \(\varepsilon_0E_1/(1 + \Omega^2\tau^2)\) with \(E_1 = E_\infty\). The difference falls like \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\). At \(t = 5\tau\) it is \(0{,}5\cdot 0{,}0067 = 0{,}0034\), and the curves coincide in the figure. From there on the stress is the one of definition 20.32. The three blackwhite dots are the check of the computation in step 5 of the proof: the hereditary integral, computed by the trapezoidal sum on \(40\,000\) pieces, gives at \(t/\tau = 0{,}5\), \(2\) and \(7\) the values \(1{,}379926\), \(-1{,}011201\) and \(0{,}802816\), and formula (20.26) gives the same to six digits.

What do \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) mean in terms of energy? In section 20.1 we defined the loss factor by the energy lost in a period (definition 20.3). Now we check that \(\gamma\) of (20.25) is the same quantity.

Lemma 20.34 Loss per period and the loss factor of the material (izguba v periodi in faktor izgub materiala)

Let \(\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\hat E\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) with \(\hat E = E_{\mathrm{shr}} + \mathrm{i}E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) and \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\) (loop: figure 20.49). The work of the stress per unit volume in one period (definition 3.57), that is the energy that turns into heat in one period per unit volume, is

\[w_{\mathrm{izg}} = \int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\sigma\,\dot\varepsilon\,\mathrm{d}t = \pi\,E_{\mathrm{izg}}\,\varepsilon_0^2 . \tag{20.29}\]

With the stored energy \(U = \tfrac12E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0^2\) (the energy of an elastic material with modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) at the largest strain, like \(\tfrac12kX^2\) in definition 20.3) we have \(w_{\mathrm{izg}}/(2\pi U) = \gamma\).

Proof

We must show (20.29) with integrals of sine and cosine over a period.

  1. From \(\hat E\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = (E_{\mathrm{shr}} + \mathrm{i}E_{\mathrm{izg}})(\cos\Omega t + \mathrm{i}\sin\Omega t)\) the real part is \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin\Omega t)\). The derivative of the strain is \(\dot\varepsilon = -\Omega\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t\) (theorem 8.13). The first term of the stress is the stress on the line, the second is the departure from it, which at \(\varepsilon = 0\) equals \(\pm E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\).
  2. The product is \(\sigma\dot\varepsilon = -\Omega\varepsilon_0^2\big(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin^2\Omega t\big)\). By lemma 9.72 (item 3 with \(a = 0\)) the integral of the first term is zero, by item 2 we have \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\sin^2\Omega t\,\mathrm{d}t = T_{\mathrm{p}}/2\). The first term is the work on the line: what the stress does on the way out to \(\varepsilon_0\), the triangle \(U\), it gets back on the way to zero, so nothing is left after a period. The second term is the area that the loop encloses.
  3. Therefore \(w_{\mathrm{izg}} = \Omega\varepsilon_0^2E_{\mathrm{izg}}T_{\mathrm{p}}/2 = \pi E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0^2\), because \(\Omega T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi\). The quotient with \(2\pi U = \pi E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0^2\) is \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_{\mathrm{shr}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The form \(\gamma = W/(2\pi U)\) is definition 20.3. CK (PDF p. 127) reads the loss of viscous damping per period, \(\pi c\Omega U^2\), as the area of the ellipse of force against displacement, and introduces \(\gamma\) in (4.79) (PDF p. 129).

The loss is therefore proportional to \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), not to the whole of \(\hat E\): the complex number carries two roles, storage and loss, and each has its own part. This split can be seen in figure 20.49.

We build the figure as at a board. Horizontally we draw the \(\varepsilon\) axis and vertically the \(\sigma\) axis. If the material were elastic with modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), the point \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\) would move along the line through the origin with slope \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), since then \(\sigma = E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\). The strain oscillates between \(-\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\), which we mark with the distance \(\varepsilon_0\) and the vertical dashed lines where the line reaches the extreme positions. For our material the stress \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin\Omega t)\) is not only \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\): the added term \(-E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t = E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\cos(\Omega t + \pi/2)\) leads the strain by a quarter of a period, since it reaches its largest value a quarter of a period before the strain does. So the point does not run along the line but along a loop. Since \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) (lemma 8.11, item 1), we have

\[\Big(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon}{E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0}\Big)^2 = 1 . \tag{20.30}\]

In the coordinates \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\) this is an ellipse with semi-axes \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\). In the plane \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\) adding \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\) tilts it so that it lies along the line. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) we have \(\sigma = \pm E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\): these are the orange points. Each lies \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}5\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) from the line, so there the loop is \(2E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) wide. The point travels clockwise, opposite to figure 9.83. That figure shows the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\) with which the dashpot acts on the mass, while here we have the stress with which the surroundings pull on the material. By the law of action and reaction the two have opposite signs: the part of the stress that loses energy is \(-E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t = (E_{\mathrm{izg}}/\Omega)\,\dot\varepsilon\), proportional to \(+\dot\varepsilon\) and not to \(-\dot q\). The opposite sign mirrors the loop across the horizontal axis and reverses the direction of travel. The area of this ellipse is \(\pi\cdot\varepsilon_0\cdot E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = 1{,}5708\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0^2\) (the map \((\varepsilon, \sigma) \mapsto (\varepsilon, \sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon)\), which tilts the ellipse, has determinant \(1\) and does not change the area) and it equals the loss (20.29): both routes give the same number. The stored energy is the area of the grey triangle under the line, \(U = \tfrac12\cdot\varepsilon_0\cdot E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}75\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0^2\), and \(\gamma = 1{,}5708/(2\pi\cdot 0{,}75) = 0{,}3333\).

Why does the loop have a width at all? We look at the branch of the standard linear solid, its Maxwell element with \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\). It has a spring \(E_1\) and a dashpot \(E_1\tau\) in series. By step 5 of the proof the stress of the branch has the amplitude \(E_1\varepsilon_0\,\Omega\tau/\sqrt{1 + \Omega^2\tau^2}\), and the dashpot stretches with a rate whose amplitude is (the stress of the branch divided by its coefficient \(E_1\tau\)) \(\Omega\varepsilon_0/\sqrt{1 + \Omega^2\tau^2}\). The power of the dashpot is force times velocity (definition 8.59), so the dashpot loses much energy only when both are large at once. Figure 20.50 shows both as lengths: the stretch of the spring, which is the stress of the branch divided by \(E_1\), and the stroke of the dashpot, which is its rate divided by \(\Omega\). At \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\) the stress of the branch is \(0{,}0995\,E_1\varepsilon_0\) (short bar under the spring) and the rate of the dashpot is \(0{,}995\,\Omega\varepsilon_0\) (long arrow under the dashpot): the dashpot moves with almost the whole rate of the strain, but with almost no force, since the branch has time to give way. At \(\Omega\tau = 10\) the stress of the branch is \(0{,}995\,E_1\varepsilon_0\) (long arrow under the spring) and the rate only \(0{,}0995\,\Omega\varepsilon_0\) (short bar under the dashpot): the force hardly moves the dashpot, so the spring takes almost all the stretch of the branch. In the middle, at \(\Omega\tau = 1\), both are \(0{,}7071\) of their size (spring, dashpot), and the loss is largest.

We read the figure row by row. Each row has the same branch, a spring \(E_1\) and a dashpot \(E_1\tau\) in series. Both carry the same stress, and their stretches add up to the stretch of the branch. The stroke of the dashpot lags the stretch of the spring by a quarter of a period: the rate of the dashpot is proportional to the stress, and the stress to the stretch of the spring, so the dashpot is farthest out when the stress passes through zero. So the amplitudes do not add like numbers but like the legs of a right triangle, \(0{,}0995^2 + 0{,}9950^2 = 1\). On the right we draw this. The sides of the rectangle are the two amplitudes, the diagonal is \(\varepsilon_0\) and its end lies on the arc with radius \(\varepsilon_0\). The loss of the branch in a period is, by lemma 20.34 and equations (20.28), equal to \(\pi E_1\varepsilon_0^2\,\Omega\tau/(1 + \Omega^2\tau^2)\), that is \(\pi E_1\) times the area of the rectangle. In the first row the rectangle is lying and thin with the area \(0{,}099\,\varepsilon_0^2\), in the third it is standing and thin with the same area, in the middle one it is a square with the area \(0{,}5\,\varepsilon_0^2\). Among rectangles with the same diagonal the square has the largest area, because \(ab \le (a^2 + b^2)/2\). So the loss of the branch is largest at \(\Omega\tau = 1\). This is the view by hand and eye of item 3 of corollary 20.36, which follows.

Example 20.35 Complex modulus of the standard solid (kompleksni modul standardnega trdnika)

For a standard linear solid with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) (a model, not a substance, as in section 20.4, curves in figure 20.51) we have \(N = 1\), \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty = E_\infty\) and \(x = \Omega\tau\). From equations (20.28) we get \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}/E_\infty = 1 + x^2/(1 + x^2)\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_\infty = x/(1 + x^2)\) and \(\gamma = x/(1 + 2x^2)\). For three frequencies:

\(\Omega\tau\) \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}/E_\infty\) \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_\infty\) \(\gamma\)
\(0{,}1\) \(1{,}0099\) \(0{,}0990\) \(0{,}0980\)
\(1\) \(1{,}5000\) \(0{,}5000\) \(0{,}3333\)
\(10\) \(1{,}9901\) \(0{,}0990\) \(0{,}0498\)

Source: The computation is in num-06.py, SymPy and NumPy. The model is the book's choice.

Slowly (\(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\)) the material behaves almost like an elastic material with modulus \(E_\infty \approx E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), quickly (\(\Omega\tau = 10\)) again like an elastic material, but with a stiffer modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \to E_0 = 2E_\infty\). Between the two, \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) climbs from \(E_\infty\) to \(E_0\), as the \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) curve of the next figure shows, and the \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) curve has a hump in it.

We read the figure from top to bottom. The axes are on a logarithmic scale, because the frequencies differ by decades. The upper curve \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) starts at \(1\) and ends at \(2\), in units of \(E_\infty\). Below it is \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), which is close to zero at both ends. At the bottom is the loss factor \(\gamma\), the quotient of the two, with a peak between the decades, and the three points of the table are marked on it. The dashed curve, the point \(A\) and the blue bars by the peak are explained below, where we need them. This quotient is just what the model of section 20.3 needs. Where is the peak and how high is it?

Corollary 20.36 Peak of the loss factor of the standard solid (vrh faktorja izgub standardnega trdnika)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + (E_0 - E_\infty)\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) with \(E_0 > E_\infty > 0\) and \(x = \Omega\tau\) (curves: figure 20.51). Then:

  1. \(\gamma(\Omega) = \dfrac{E_0 - E_\infty}{E_\infty/x + E_0x}\) (lower curve).
  2. \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \gamma_{\max} = \dfrac{E_0 - E_\infty}{2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}}\), with equality exactly at \(x = \sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) (peak). With the retardation time \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau E_0/E_\infty\) of definition 20.26 this is \(\Omega = 1/\sqrt{\tau\,\tau_\varepsilon}\).
  3. \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega) \le (E_0 - E_\infty)/2\), with equality exactly at \(x = 1\) (peak of the \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) curve).
Proof

We must show three items: the first by computation from theorem 20.33, the second and third by the inequality of the square of a difference.

  1. With \(N = 1\) and \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\) we have by equations (20.28) \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E_\infty + E_1x^2/(1 + x^2) = (E_\infty + E_0x^2)/(1 + x^2)\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E_1x/(1 + x^2)\). The quotient is \(\gamma = E_1x/(E_\infty + E_0x^2)\), which after dividing by \(x\) gives item 1.
  2. The square of a difference is nonnegative: \(\big(\sqrt{E_0x} - \sqrt{E_\infty/x}\big)^2 \ge 0\), so \(E_0x + E_\infty/x \ge 2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}\), and equality holds exactly when \(E_0x = E_\infty/x\), that is \(x^2 = E_\infty/E_0\). The denominator of item 1 is thus at least \(2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}\), which gives the inequality. In the figure this is the peak of the lower curve, and in the figure of the denominators the bottom of the sum above the crossing of the terms.
  3. At \(x = \sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) we have \(\Omega = (1/\tau)\sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) and \(\tau\tau_\varepsilon = \tau^2E_0/E_\infty\), so \(1/\sqrt{\tau\tau_\varepsilon} = \Omega\).
  4. From \((1 - x)^2 \ge 0\) we have \(1 + x^2 \ge 2x\), so \(x/(1 + x^2) \le 1/2\) with equality at \(x = 1\). We multiply by \(E_1\). In the figure this is the peak with the value \(0{,}5\), since there \(E_1 = E_\infty\), and in the figure of the denominators the bottom of the sum \(1/x + x\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The peak at \(x = 1/\sqrt2\) and the value \(0{,}35355\) for \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) are confirmed by SymPy (num-06.py).

For \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) the peak is at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}7071\) with the value \(\gamma_{\max} = 1/(2\sqrt2) = 0{,}35355\) (figure 20.51). Here is also a case that almost succeeds: the peak of the loss modulus is at \(\Omega\tau = 1\) (item 3) with the value \(0{,}5\,E_\infty\), and there \(\gamma = 0{,}3333\), less than \(0{,}35355\). The peaks differ because the storage modulus in the denominator of the quotient between them grows, from \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = 1{,}3333\,E_\infty\) at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}7071\) to \(1{,}5\,E_\infty\) at \(\Omega\tau = 1\), and the quotient decreases although the numerator still grows a little.

Why the peaks lie just there is also shown by the denominators. By item 1, \(\gamma\) equals \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\) divided by \(E_\infty/x + E_0x\), and by step 1 of the proof \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E_1x/(1 + x^2)\) equals \(E_1\) divided by \(1/x + x\). A quotient with a constant numerator is largest where its denominator is smallest, so we draw both denominators (figure 20.52).

On the axes of both halves we have \(x = \Omega\tau\) horizontally and the value of the denominator vertically, both on a logarithmic scale. On it a term of the form \(a/x\) is a line with slope \(-1\) and a term of the form \(ax\) a line with slope \(+1\), since \(\log(a/x) = \log a - \log x\) and \(\log(ax) = \log a + \log x\). On the left is the falling term \(E_\infty/x\), large for slow stretching, and the rising term \(E_0x\), large for fast stretching. Their sum is almost equal to the larger term at both ends, and in between it has a bottom. The bottom lies above the crossing of the lines, where \(E_\infty/x = E_0x\), that is at \(x = \sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\). This is step 2 of the proof. The product of the terms equals \(E_0E_\infty\) at every \(x\), so the sum equals \(2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}\) increased by the square of the difference \(\big(\sqrt{E_0x} - \sqrt{E_\infty/x}\big)^2\). This square is zero exactly where the terms are equal and positive elsewhere, so the sum is smallest there, \(2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty} = 2{,}83\,E_\infty\) at \(x = 0{,}7071\). The loss factor is therefore largest there, \(\gamma_{\max} = E_1/(2{,}83\,E_\infty) = 0{,}35355\), since here \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty = E_\infty\).

On the right is the same for the loss modulus. The falling term \(1/x\) is the same line as on the left, while the rising term \(x\) is half as high as the \(E_0x = 2x\) on the left (in units of \(E_\infty\)). The sum \(1/x + x\) has its bottom above the crossing at \(x = 1\), with the value \(2\), so there \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E_1/2 = 0{,}5\,E_\infty\) is largest (step 4 of the proof). The two halves differ only in the rising term: the line \(E_0x\), twice as high, crosses the falling one earlier, at \(x^2 = 1/2\), that is a factor \(\sqrt2\) further left.

The position of the peak has an explanation in the two times of the standard linear solid. The frequency \(1/\tau\) tells how fast the stress relaxes at constant strain, the frequency \(1/\tau_\varepsilon\) how fast the strain settles at constant stress (section 20.4). For \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) we have \(1/\tau_\varepsilon = 0{,}5/\tau\), and the peak at \(0{,}7071/\tau\) is their geometric mean, since \(\sqrt{1\cdot 0{,}5} = 0{,}7071\). On a logarithmic axis the geometric mean lies halfway: the peak is equally far from \(0{,}5\) and from \(1\).

The standard linear solid therefore has a peak, and above it and below it the losses fall. The Kelvin-Voigt element, which in section 20.4 is the second simple model, is different. Its law is \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\dot\varepsilon\) with \(\eta = E\tau\) (definition 20.24, where \(\tau = \eta/E\) is called the retardation time \(\tau_\varepsilon\)), without memory, so there are no transient terms and we get the complex modulus directly.

Lemma 20.37 Complex modulus of the Kelvin-Voigt element (kompleksni modul Kelvin-Voigtovega člena)

Let \(\varepsilon(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) and \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + E\tau\dot\varepsilon\) with \(E, \tau > 0\) (comparison with the standard linear solid: figure 20.51). Then for every \(t\)

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(E(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau)\,\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) , \tag{20.31}\]

so \(\hat E = E(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau)\), \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E\Omega\tau\) and \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\).

Proof

We must show only the derivative of the strain.

  1. By theorem 9.34 (item 3) we have \(\dot\varepsilon = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\).
  2. Since the real part is linear, \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\big((E + E\tau\,\mathrm{i}\Omega)\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\). This is (20.31). From \(E + \mathrm{i}\,E\Omega\tau\) we read \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E\Omega\tau\) and \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The law of the element is in definition 20.24.

The loss factor \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\) grows with \(\Omega\) without bound, because the loss modulus \(E\Omega\tau\) grows while the storage modulus \(E\) stays. A comparison with the standard linear solid from example 20.35 shows the difference: at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\) the Kelvin-Voigt \(\gamma\) is \(0{,}1\) (standard linear solid \(0{,}0980\)), at \(1\) it is \(1\) (against \(0{,}3333\)), at \(10\) it is \(10\) (against \(0{,}0498\)). The Kelvin-Voigt element does not stiffen under fast stretching, but stays at the same modulus \(E\) and the dashpot holds it back more and more: the dashed curve \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\) exceeds the peak of the standard linear solid already at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}3536\) and at \(\Omega\tau = 1\), where the figure no longer shows it, is three times as high as the curve of the standard linear solid (\(1\) against \(0{,}3333\)).

We can check the same on a dashpot that we know. For cantilever \(A\) (section 9.6) the dashpot \(c = 35{,}4175\) N s/m is parallel to the spring \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, which is a Kelvin-Voigt element with \(\tau = c/k = 5{,}647\cdot 10^{-4}\) s. At \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s we get \(\gamma = \Omega\tau = 0{,}0200\), and by lemma 20.4 we have \(\gamma = 2\zeta r = 2\cdot 0{,}01\cdot 1 = 0{,}0200\). The same number from two directions. At \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}02\), at the point \(A\) close to the left edge of the figure, the Kelvin-Voigt element and the standard linear solid have almost the same \(\gamma\) (each \(0{,}0200\)), since there \(\gamma = x/(1 + 2x^2) \approx x\). A Kelvin-Voigt material with the same \(\tau\) in all elements also gives damping proportional to stiffness, \(\mathbf{C} = a_1\mathbf{K}\) of definition 10.62: the coefficient \(a_1\) is the time \(\tau\), and the loss factor \(\gamma = a_1\Omega\) grows with \(\Omega\), as the lemma says.

Does any Prony material have a constant \(\gamma\), as section 20.3 assumes (figure 20.55)? The answer is no, on the whole frequency axis. The reason lies in the two functions of which, by equations (20.28), both moduli are made (figure 20.53).

On the axes we have \(x = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) horizontally and the value of the function vertically, both on a logarithmic scale, so that both ends can be seen. The blackwhite curve is \(x/(1 + x^2)\), the share of term \(j\) in \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), divided by \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\). On the left it hugs the line \(x\), on the right the line \(1/x\), and it is nowhere above them: at \(x = 0{,}01\) and at \(x = 100\) it is \(0{,}01\), and at most it reaches \(\tfrac12\) at \(x = 1\). The blue curve is \(x^2/(1 + x^2)\), the share of term \(j\) in \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} - E_\infty\), divided by \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\): on the left it falls even faster, like \(x^2\), and on the right it stays above the level \(\tfrac12\). The lemma adds these bounds up over the terms.

Lemma 20.38 A Prony series has no constant loss factor (Pronyjeva vrsta nima stalnega faktorja izgub)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus (20.23) (curves: figure 20.55) with finite \(N \ge 1\), \(E_{\mathrm{j}}, \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), \(\tau_{\min} = \min_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\tau_{\max} = \max_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). Then:

  1. If \(E_\infty > 0\), then \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty\) for every \(\Omega > 0\), and for \(\Omega \ge 1/\tau_{\min}\) we have \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \dfrac{\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{\Omega\,(E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}})}\). So \(\gamma \to 0\) as \(\Omega \to 0\) and as \(\Omega \to \infty\), as figure 20.55 shows left and right of the band, and in the example the solid under its bounds.
  2. If \(E_\infty = 0\) (a liquid), then for \(0 < \Omega \le 1/\tau_{\max}\) we have \(\gamma(\Omega) \ge 1/(2\Omega\tau_{\max})\), so \(\gamma \to \infty\) as \(\Omega \to 0\) (liquid above its bound).

In neither case is \(\gamma\) constant on \((0, \infty)\) (figure 20.55, no curve stays on the level \(c\)).

Idea

For each term, \(x/(1 + x^2)\) is at most \(x\) and at most \(1/x\) (blackwhite curve under the grey lines), which is small for small and for large \(x\) respectively. So the loss modulus is small at both ends of the frequency axis, while the storage modulus stays at least \(E_\infty\). The result is seen at the edges of figure 20.55.

Proof

We must show the estimates from theorem 20.33 (equations (20.28)) and the conclusion that \(\gamma\) is not constant. Let \(x_{\mathrm{j}} = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. Since \(1 + x^2 \ge 1\) and \(1 + x^2 \ge x^2\), we have \(x/(1 + x^2) \le x\) (left line) and \(x/(1 + x^2) \le 1/x\) (right line). Therefore \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \le (1/\Omega)\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. For \(E_\infty > 0\) we have \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \ge E_\infty\), so \(\gamma \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty\) (rising bound).
  3. For \(\Omega \ge 1/\tau_{\min}\) every \(x_{\mathrm{j}} \ge 1\), so \(x_{\mathrm{j}}^2/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \ge \tfrac12\) (blue curve above the level \(\tfrac12\)) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \ge E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\). With the estimate of step 1 the second inequality of item 1 follows (falling bound).
  4. For \(E_\infty = 0\) and \(\Omega \le 1/\tau_{\max}\) every \(x_{\mathrm{j}} \le 1\), so \(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \le 2\) and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \ge x_{\mathrm{j}}/2\) (left of \(x = 1\) the blackwhite curve does not fall below half of the line \(x\)). Therefore \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \ge \tfrac12\Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). At the same time \(x_{\mathrm{j}}^2/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \le x_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \le \Omega^2\tau_{\max}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \le \Omega^2\tau_{\max}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). The quotient is at least \(1/(2\Omega\tau_{\max})\) (bound under the curve of the liquid).
  5. Since \(N \ge 1\) and \(E_{\mathrm{j}}, \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), both \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) are positive for every \(\Omega > 0\), so \(\gamma(\Omega) > 0\). A constant \(\gamma = c\) would have \(c > 0\), but by item 1 \(\gamma \to 0\) and by item 2 \(\gamma \to \infty\). Therefore in neither case is \(\gamma\) constant (level \(c\), which both curves leave).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

Let us show both items of the lemma on one series (figure 20.54). We take three terms with \(E_{\mathrm{j}} = 0{,}2\) and times \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\), \(0{,}1\) and \(0{,}01\) (time in an arbitrary unit, \(\Omega\) in its inverse), so \(\tau_{\max} = 1\) and \(\tau_{\min} = 0{,}01\). Once we add the firm spring \(E_\infty = 1\) (a solid), once not (a liquid, \(E_\infty = 0\)).

On the axes we have \(\Omega\) from \(0{,}01\) to \(10^4\) horizontally and \(\gamma\) vertically, both on a logarithmic scale, on which the bounds of the lemma, powers of \(\Omega\), are lines. On the left is the loss factor of the solid, computed by equations (20.28). Above it lies the rising bound of item 1, \(\Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty = 0{,}222\,\Omega\), since \(0{,}2\cdot(1 + 0{,}1 + 0{,}01) = 0{,}222\). At \(\Omega = 0{,}01\) we have \(\gamma = 0{,}00222\), as much as the bound, because there all \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are small and each term lies almost on its line \(x\) of figure 20.53. From \(\Omega = 1/\tau_{\min} = 100\) on, the curve also lies under the falling bound of item 1, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\big/\big(\Omega(E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}})\big) = 17{,}08/\Omega\), since \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = 0{,}2\cdot(1 + 10 + 100) = 22{,}2\) and \(E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}} = 1 + \tfrac12\cdot 0{,}6 = 1{,}3\), and their quotient is \(17{,}08\). At \(\Omega = 10^4\) this bound is \(0{,}00171\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}00139\). Both lines go down towards the edges of the figure, so the \(\gamma\) of the solid under them goes to zero on both sides.

On the right is the loss factor of the liquid. Up to \(\Omega = 1/\tau_{\max} = 1\) it lies above the bound of item 2, \(1/(2\Omega\tau_{\max}) = 1/(2\Omega)\), which rises to the left: at \(\Omega = 0{,}01\) the bound is \(50\) and \(\gamma = 109{,}9\). Without the spring \(E_\infty\) the storage modulus falls like \(\Omega^2\) at slow motion, while the loss modulus falls only like \(\Omega\) (step 4 of the proof), so their quotient grows without bound.

The level \(c = 0{,}05\) stands for any constant value. The curve of the solid is above it only in the middle part of the axis, the curve of the liquid only in the left part, and neither stays on it. This is step 5 of the proof: a constant \(\gamma = c > 0\) would have to lie on this level along the whole axis, but the curves leave it, the first downwards on both sides, the second upwards on the left.

The lemma says (figure 20.55) that the constant \(\gamma\) of section 20.3 is not a property of any Prony material on the whole frequency axis: at slow motion the material (since it has the firm spring \(E_\infty\)) is almost elastic, at fast motion just as much, and a liquid has more and more loss at slow motion. But it is possible to approximate a constant \(\gamma\) on a band of frequencies. We take \(N\) terms with times \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) spread evenly on a logarithmic scale from \(1\) to \(0{,}01\) (for \(N = 1\) only \(\tau_1 = 0{,}1\), time in an arbitrary unit, \(\Omega\) in its inverse), \(E_\infty = 1\), and look for weights \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) such that \(\gamma = 0{,}1\) on the band \(1 \le \Omega \le 100\). The condition \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0{,}1\,E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is by equations (20.28) linear in \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\),

\[\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N}E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{x_{\mathrm{j}} - 0{,}1\,x_{\mathrm{j}}^2}{1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2} = 0{,}1\,E_\infty , \qquad x_{\mathrm{j}} = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}} ,\]

which we require at 400 points spread evenly on a logarithmic scale and solve by the method of least squares.

In the figure there are the axes, \(\Omega\) horizontally and \(\gamma\) vertically, and the band with the target \(\gamma = 0{,}1\). Above them is the smaller graph of the storage modulus, to which we return in the next paragraph. The curve for \(N = 1\), so the standard linear solid, has a peak of \(0{,}1345\) in the band and \(0{,}0233\) at its edge, that is \(+35\ \%\) and \(-77\ \%\) relative to the target. Three terms follow the target in the band between \(0{,}0952\) and \(0{,}1047\), that is \(-4{,}8\ \%\) and \(+4{,}7\ \%\), and five terms between \(0{,}0952\) and \(0{,}1018\), \(-4{,}8\ \%\) and \(+1{,}8\ \%\). All weights are positive (for \(N = 3\): \(E_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty = 0{,}1847\), \(0{,}1792\) and \(0{,}2574\), for \(N = 5\) at least \(0{,}0552\)), so this is a real material (lemma 20.38 has the condition \(E_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\)). Outside the band all three curves fall, as the lemma requires: for \(N = 3\) we have \(\gamma(0{,}1) = 0{,}0203\) and \(\gamma(1000) = 0{,}0170\), that is a fifth and a sixth of the target. The bounds of the lemma hold, again for \(N = 3\): at \(\Omega = 0{,}01\) the upper bound of item 1 is \(0{,}00205\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}00205\) (the bound is almost reached, because all \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are small), at \(\Omega = 10^4\) the bound is \(0{,}00211\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}00171\).

The band is therefore an approximation and not an equality, and its price has two sides. The first is the storage modulus: for \(N = 3\) we have \(E_0/E_\infty = 1{,}621\) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is not constant on the band, but grows from \(1{,}094\,E_\infty\) to \(1{,}491\,E_\infty\), so by \(36\ \%\). The model \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) of section 20.3 has both constant, which is the second idealization that the band brings with it. The other side is a gain: the stress of a Prony material at time \(t\) depends, by the hereditary integral of section 20.5, only on the strain at times \(s \le t\), so it does not have the problem that hysteretic damping had in time (lemma 20.18). For a Prony material a constant \(\gamma\) therefore makes sense as a description of the frequency response on the band in which the structure moves, and not as a law of the substance.

In section 20.7 we will insert \(\hat E(\Omega)\), that is \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) on the band, into the stiffness matrices of elements. There \(\gamma\) will no longer be the number of one substance, but a property of each element.

20.7 Damping in the finite element model

Chapter 10 took the damping matrix \(\mat C\) as given: Rayleigh damping (definition 10.62) or modal damping (definition 10.64), where we choose the ratios of the modes. With finite elements a second question arises: can we assemble \(\mat C\) from elements, as we assembled the stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) (theorem 7.13) and the mass matrix \(\mat M\) (section 10.8.3)? The sources are cautious. CK (PDF p. 321) says that the damping matrix could in principle be derived by finite element procedures, but the material properties are not known well enough and most of the damping comes from joints and non-structural parts, so the damping is usually determined for the whole system. BATHE (PDF p. 813) says that the matrix \(\mat C\) cannot as a rule be assembled from element matrices as the mass and stiffness matrices are, and that it is introduced to capture approximately the total loss of energy.

Still, we know two mechanisms that can be written for one element: a material that resists the rate of strain (the Kelvin-Voigt term, section 20.4), and a dashpot that is attached along the body to a resting surroundings, such as air or oil (section 20.1). There are three questions. What matrix does each of them give for one element? When is the assembled matrix Rayleigh damping, that is classical, and what happens if it is not? And what do we do with damping that we know only for harmonic motion, hysteretic (section 20.3) and frequency-dependent material (section 20.6)? We are guided by frame A from section 10.1: two floors with mass \(m = 500\) kg, stiffness of each storey \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, natural frequencies \(\omega_1 = 19{,}578\) and \(\omega_2 = 51{,}257\) 1/s, and the modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\) from section 10.3.4 (in kg\(^{-1/2}\)).

20.7.1 Damping matrix of one element

Take a bar element with two nodes and length \(h\) (definition 7.1), with constant \(EA\) and \(\rho A\), and a beam element (section 12.1). In both the field on the element is \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (for the beam \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\)), where the nodal displacements \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}(t)\) are functions of time and the shape functions are functions of position. How would we get the damping force on the nodes from this?

We draw the element as a line between two nodes that move by \(d_1\) and \(d_2\). Between them is the length of the element \(h\). On the nodes the surroundings act with the forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). They start at the nodes and point outward, because they stretch the element if we pull (lemma 7.9). The first mechanism is the material of the element. For the Kelvin-Voigt element (definition 20.24) the stress is the sum of two parts, \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\dot\varepsilon = E\,(\varepsilon + \tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon)\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the strain, \(\eta\) the viscosity and \(\tau_\varepsilon = \eta/E\) the retardation time (čas zakasnitve) in seconds. The first part is the spring, as in chapter 7, the second is the dashpot in parallel with it, because both deform by the same strain and their stresses add. A dashpot feels the rate of stretching, so we also draw the velocities of the nodes \(\dot d_1\) and \(\dot d_2\) as blue arrows. The right one is longer than the left one: the right node runs away from the left one, the element stretches at the rate \(\dot d_2 - \dot d_1\), and since strain is elongation divided by length, the strain rate is \(\dot\varepsilon = (\dot d_2 - \dot d_1)/h\). The second mechanism is the external dashpot. We draw it below the bar and attach it to the resting surroundings, because such a dashpot (air, oil, definition 9.1) acts on every piece of the bar with the force \(-c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\) per unit length. The constant \(c_{\mathrm{z}}\) has the unit N s/m\(^2\). Above the bar we draw the velocities of its pieces \(\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\). They grow evenly from \(\dot d_1\) on the left to \(\dot d_2\) on the right, because the field between the nodes is linear. Every dashpot therefore pulls its piece backward, against the velocity, and the right one pulls hardest, because its piece is the fastest.

Why the matrices of both mechanisms are so simple is told by the next lemma. For the beam the same conclusions hold, because we only replace the energy of stretching by the energy of curvature.

Lemma 20.39 Damping matrix of an element (matrika dušenja elementa)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite element of a bar (definition 7.1) or of a beam (definition 12.3) with stiffness matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 7.5, lemma 12.4) and mass matrix \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 10.47, lemma 12.43) and with constant \(EA\) and \(\rho A\) (for the beam \(EI\) and \(\rho A\)). Let \(\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the row of shape functions (for the beam \(\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\)), \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) the field on the element and \(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) the column of nodal velocities. Then:

  1. If the material is Kelvin-Voigt, \(\sigma = E\,(\varepsilon + \tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon)\) with constant \(\tau_\varepsilon > 0\), the virtual work of the viscous part of the stress at a virtual displacement \(\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) equals \(-\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{20.32}\]
  2. If an external dashpot with force \(-c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\) per unit length with constant \(c_{\mathrm{z}} \ge 0\) acts on the element, the virtual work of this force equals \(-\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = c_{\mathrm{z}}\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{c_{\mathrm{z}}}{\rho A}\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{20.33}\]
  3. Both matrices \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) (material, external dashpot) are symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), for \(\tau_\varepsilon > 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{z}} > 0\) the matrix \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) of point 2 is even positive definite, and the matrix of point 1 has the same kernel as \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\).
Proof
